title: حِكَايَةُ الْحَمَّالِ وَ الثَّلٰثِ بَنَاتِ
titleEn: The Porter and the Three Ladies, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 64–73 (continuing directly from nights-09, whose text ends as the drunken women's repeated genital-naming game with the porter is cut short by dawn), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 10 continues the Story of the Porter and the Three Ladies. Three one-eyed wandering qalandars arrive at the sisters' door seeking a night's shelter and are admitted, like the porter before them, on condition that they ask no question about what they see. Soon after, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid himself arrives in merchant disguise with his vizier Jafar and his executioner Masrur, drawn by the music, and talks his way in under the same condition. As the wine takes hold, the lady of the house performs a ritual whipping of two black bitches, weeping over each in turn and kissing her afterward — a spectacle none of the guests dares ask about. Her sister, called Khushkasha in the household, then sings three love-songs in succession; at each one a different sister swoons, tears her own clothes, and is revealed to bear the marks of an old beating. Devoured by curiosity but bound by their word, the Caliph's party debates who should risk asking after the mystery, and settles on the porter. His question breaks the house's one rule: the lady accuses her guests of ingratitude and summons armed slaves to bind them all for execution. The porter alone protests his innocence — he blames the nosy qalandars — and begs for mercy in verse; the lady's resulting laughter is the last thing dawn allows before it cuts Shahrazad off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language toward Classical Arabic here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about violence (the whipping of the two bitches, the threat of summary execution) and is translated that way, without euphemism.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْعَاشِرَةُ قَالَتْ لَهَا أُخْتُهَا دُنْيَازَادُ أَتِمِّي لَنَا حَدِيثَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānat al-laylat al-ʿāshirat qālat lahā ukhtuhā Dunyāzād atimmī lanā ḥadīthaki
sentences.l: Then, when it was the tenth night, her sister Dunyazad said to her, ‘Finish for us your story.’
sentences.i: When the tenth night came, her sister Dunyazad said to her, ‘Finish your tale for us.’

sentences.t: قُلْتُ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: qultu ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: I said: ‘With love and honor.’
sentences.i: ‘Gladly,’ I said.
sentences.n: The teller slips from third person (‘she said’) into Shahrazad’s own first-person voice (‘I said’) here — a recurring feature of how these nights open, not an error.

sentences.t: يَبْلُغُنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْبَنَاتِ مَازَالُوا يَقُولُونَ لِلْحَمَّالِ زُبُّكَ أَيْرُكَ خَازُوقُكَ وَ يَعْنُقُ إِلَى أَنِ اشْتَفَى قَلْبُهُ مِنْهُنَّ
sentences.tr: yablughunī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-banāti mā zālū yaqūlūna li-al-ḥammāli zubbuka ayruka khāzūquka wa-yaʿnuqu ilā ani-shtafā qalbuhu minhunna
sentences.l: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the girls kept saying to the porter: ‘Your penis! Your rod! Your stake!’ — while he embraced, until his heart was satisfied of them.
sentences.i: As I have heard, O fortunate King, the girls kept crying to the porter, ‘Your cock! Your prick! Your pole!’ — hugging him tight until his heart had had its fill of them.
sentences.n: The feminine plural subject al-banāt (‘the girls’) here takes masculine-plural verbs (zālū, yaqūlūna) rather than the classical feminine forms — a routine leveling in this text’s Middle Arabic, not corrected below.

sentences.t: وَهُمْ يَتَضَاحَكُونَ إِلَى أَنْ قَالُوا لَهُ يَا أَخِينَا مَا اسْمُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-hum yataḍāḥakūna ilā an qālū lahu yā akhīnā mā ismuhu
sentences.l: while they were laughing together, until they said to him, ‘O our brother, what is its name?’
sentences.i: all the while laughing together, until they said, ‘Brother, what do you call it?’
sentences.n: ‘Its name’ keeps up the joke — they mean the member just apostrophized, not the porter himself.

sentences.t: قَالَ مَا تَعْرِفُونَ مَا اسْمُهُ
sentences.tr: qāla mā taʿrifūna mā ismuhu
sentences.l: He said: ‘Do you not know what its name is?’
sentences.i: ‘Don’t you know its name?’ he said.

sentences.t: قُلْنَ لَا
sentences.tr: qulna lā
sentences.l: They (f.) said: ‘No.’
sentences.i: ‘No,’ they said.

sentences.t: قَالَ هَٰذَا الْبَغْلُ الْكَسُورُ يَرْعِي حَبَقَ الْجُسُورِ وَيَسُفُّ السِّمْسِمَ الْمَقْشُورَ وَيَبَاتُ فِي خَانِ أَبُومَنْصُورٍ
sentences.tr: qāla hādhā al-baghlu al-kasūru yarʿī ḥabaqa al-jusūri wa-yasuffu al-simsima al-maqshūra wa-yabātu fī khāni Abūmanṣūrin
sentences.l: He said: ‘This is the broken-down mule — he grazes on the basil of the bridges, and snuffles up peeled sesame, and lodges at the inn of Abu Mansur.’
sentences.i: ‘This,’ he said, ‘is the broken-down mule: he grazes on bridge-rail clover, gulps down peeled sesame, and beds down at the Inn of Abu Mansur.’
sentences.n: الكسور as printed does not match the expected adjective al-kasīr (‘broken-down, lame’); it is kept exactly as archived and read that way. The kunya ‘Abu Mansur’ is printed fused as one word and left undeclined (archive: ابومنصور) rather than corrected to the expected genitive أبي منصور.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكُوا حَتَّى انْقَلَبُوا عَلَى قَفَاهُمْ وَعَادُوا إِلَى مُنَادَمَتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥikū ḥattā inqalabū ʿalā qafāhum wa-ʿādū ilā munādamatihim
sentences.l: So they laughed until they turned over onto the backs of their necks, and returned to their carousing.
sentences.i: They laughed till they fell over backward, then went back to their drinking and company.

sentences.t: وَ لَمْ يَزَالُوا كَذَٰلِكَ إِلَى أَنْ أَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū ka-dhālika ilā an aqbala al-laylu ʿalayhim
sentences.l: And they did not cease being thus, until the night came upon them.
sentences.i: And so it went, until night fell upon them.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لِلْحَمَّالِ بِسْمِ اللَّٰهِ يَا سَيِّدِي قُمْ وَالْبَسْ زَرْمُوجَتَكَ وَتَوَجَّهْ وَأَوْرِينَا عَرْضَ أَكْتَافِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū li-al-ḥammāl bi-ism Allāh yā sayyidī qum wa-albas zarmūjataka wa-tawajjah wa-awrīnā ʿarḍa aktāfika
sentences.l: So they said to the porter: ‘In the name of God, O my master — rise, and put on your boots, and set off, and show us the breadth of your shoulders.’
sentences.i: So they said to the porter, ‘In God’s name, sir — up you get, boots on, and off with you: let’s see the width of your back.’
sentences.n: زرموجة is a Persian loanword for a soft riding-boot. ‘Show us the breadth of your shoulders’ is a jesting way of saying ‘be on your way’; note also that أورينا keeps the stem vowel before the object suffix (Middle Arabic), where classical grammar would give أَرِنَا.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ وَاللَّٰهِ خُرُوجُ الرُّوحِ أَهْوَنُ مِنْ خُرُوجِي مِنْ عِنْدِكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu wa-Allāhi khurūju al-rūḥi ahwanu min khurūjī min ʿindikum
sentences.l: The porter said: ‘By God, the going-out of the soul is easier than my going-out from among you.’
sentences.i: The porter said, ‘By God, giving up the ghost would be easier than leaving your company!’

sentences.t: دَعُونَا نَصِلِ اللَّيْلَ بِالنَّهَارِ وَغَدَاةَ كُلُّ مِنَّا يَرُوحُ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: daʿūnā naṣil al-layla bi-al-nahār wa-ghadāta kullu minnā yarūḥu ilā ḥāli sabīlihi
sentences.l: Let us join the night to the day, and in the morning each of us goes to the state of his own way.
sentences.i: Let’s carry the night through to morning, and then each of us can be on his way.
sentences.n: ‘To the state of his own way’ = go about his own business.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْخَشْكَاشَةُ بِحَيَاتِي عَلَيْكُمْ دَعُوهُ يُقَامُ عِنْدَنَا نَضْحَكُ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat al-Khashkāshah bi-ḥayātī ʿalaykum daʿūhu yuqām ʿindanā naḍḥak ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then Khushkasha said: ‘Upon my life, I ask of you — leave him be, let him be kept with us, [that] we may laugh at him.’
sentences.i: Then Khushkasha said, ‘On my life, leave him — let him stay the night with us, and we’ll have our laugh at him.’
sentences.n: The archive spells this speaker's name الخشكاشة here and الخوشكاشة a few lines later; both spellings are for the same person and are rendered consistently as 'Khushkasha' in translation, though the Arabic spelling itself is left exactly as printed at each occurrence.

sentences.t: فَمَنْ بَقِيَ يَعِيشُ حَتَّى نَجْتَمِعَ عَلَى مِثْلِ هَٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-man baqiya yaʿīshu ḥattā najtamiʿa ʿalā mithli hādhā
sentences.l: For who remains alive, until we gather again over the like of this?
sentences.i: Who knows if we’ll live to meet again over such an evening?

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ خَلِيعٌ ظَرِيفٌ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu khalīʿun ẓarīfun
sentences.l: For he is a rakish, witty one.
sentences.i: He’s a rogue, and good company besides.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا مَا تَبَاتُ عِنْدَنَا إِلَّا بِشَرْطِ أَنْ تَدْخُلَ تَحْتَ الْحُكْمِ وَمَهْمَا رَأَيْتَ لَا تَسْأَلْ عَنْهُ وَلَا عَنْ سَبَبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū mā tabātu ʿindanā illā bi-sharṭi an tadkhula taḥta al-ḥukm wa-mahmā ra'ayta lā tas'al ʿanhu wa-lā ʿan sababihi
sentences.l: So they said: ‘You shall not spend the night with us except on condition that you enter under the ruling; and whatever you see, do not ask about it, nor about its cause.’
sentences.i: They said, ‘You may stay the night with us on one condition only: submit to our rule. Whatever you see, ask nothing about it, and nothing about why.’

sentences.t: فَقَالَ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla naʿam
sentences.l: He said: ‘Yes.’
sentences.i: ‘Agreed,’ he said.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا قُمْ وَاقْرَأِ الْكِتَابَةَ الَّذِي عَلَى الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū qum wa-iqraʾ al-kitābata al-ladhī ʿalā al-bāb
sentences.l: So they said: ‘Rise, and read the writing that (masc.) is on the door.’
sentences.i: They said, ‘Get up and read the notice on the door.’
sentences.n: الذي (masc.) is used for the feminine noun الكتابة, where classical grammar wants التي — another Middle Arabic gender-agreement relaxation, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ إِلَى الْبَابِ فَوَجَدَ مَكْتُوبًا عَلَيْهِ بِمَاءِ الذَّهَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma ilā al-bāb fa-wajada maktūban ʿalayhi bi-māʾ al-dhahab
sentences.l: So he got up to the door, and found written upon it, in water of gold:
sentences.i: So he went to the door and found written there, in gilt letters:

sentences.t: مَنْ يَتَكَلَّمْ فِيمَا لَا يَعْنِيهِ يَسْمَعْ مَا لَا يُرْضِيهِ
sentences.tr: man yatakallam fīmā lā yaʿnīhi yasmaʿ mā lā yurḍīhi
sentences.l: Whoever speaks about what does not concern him hears what does not please him.
sentences.i: Speak of what is not your concern, and you will hear what you would rather not.
sentences.n: A rhymed house-maxim (yaʿnīhi / yurḍīhi) posted on the door; the rhyme is kept visible above rather than flattened.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ أَشْهِدُوا عَلَى أَنِّي لَا أَتَكَلَّمُ فِيمَا لَا يَعْنِينِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu ishhadū ʿalā annī lā atakallamu fīmā lā yaʿnīnī
sentences.l: The porter said: ‘Bear witness, concerning [the fact] that I will not speak of what does not concern me.’
sentences.i: The porter said, ‘Bear me witness — I will not speak of what does not concern me.’

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتِ الْخَوْشْكَاشَةُ وَجَهَّزَتْ لَهُمْ مَأْكُولًا فَأَكَلُوا
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat al-Khawshkāshah wa-jahhazat lahum ma'kūlan fa-akalū
sentences.l: Then Khushkasha rose, and prepared for them something to eat, and they ate.
sentences.i: Then Khushkasha got up and had food brought for them, and they ate.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَوْقَدُوا الشُّمُوعَ وَالْقَنَادِيلَ وَغَرَسُوا فِي الشُّمُوعِ الْعَنْبَرَ وَالْعُودَ
sentences.tr: thumma awqadū al-shumūʿa wa-al-qanādīla wa-gharasū fī al-shumūʿi al-ʿanbara wa-al-ʿūd
sentences.l: Then they lit the candles and the lamps, and planted in the candles ambergris and aloeswood.
sentences.i: Then they lit the candles and lamps, and studded the candles with ambergris and aloeswood.
sentences.n: ‘Planted’ (gharasū) is the archive’s own vivid verb for pressing lumps of ambergris and aloeswood into the burning wax so their scent fills the room.

sentences.t: وَقَعَدُوا عَلَى الشَّرَابِ بِمُذَاكَرَةِ الْأَحْبَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-qaʿadū ʿalā al-sharābi bi-mudhākarati al-aḥbāb
sentences.l: and they sat to the wine, with the mutual-recalling of loved ones,
sentences.i: and settled to their wine amid the talk of friends,

sentences.t: وَقَدْ غَيَّرُوا ذَٰلِكَ الْمَقَامَ بِغَيْرِهِ وَصَفُّوا فَاكِهَةً طَرِيَّةً وَكَذَٰلِكَ الْمَشْرُوبَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ghayyarū dhālika al-maqāma bi-ghayrihi wa-ṣaffū fākihatan ṭariyyatan wa-ka-dhālika al-mashrūb
sentences.l: and they had changed that gathering-place for another, and had set out fresh fruit, and likewise the drink,
sentences.i: having by now moved from that spot to another, with fresh fruit laid out, and drink to match,

sentences.t: وَلَا زَالُوا فِي الْأَكْلِ وَ نُقْلٍ وَضَحِكٍ وَخِدَاعٍ سَاعَةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā zālū fī al-akli wa-nuqlin wa-ḍaḥikin wa-khidāʿin sāʿatan min al-zamān
sentences.l: And they did not cease [being engaged] in eating, and dessert, and laughing, and teasing, for an hour of time.
sentences.i: And so they went on eating, snacking, laughing, and teasing one another for a good while.
sentences.n: نقل (nuql) is the dried fruit and sweets served with drink; خداع here is playful teasing, not real deceit.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا هُمْ بِالْبَابِ يُدَقُّ فَلَمْ يَنْخَرِمْ نِظَامُهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā hum bi-al-bābi yudaqqu fa-lam yankharim niẓāmuhum
sentences.l: And suddenly there they were, with the door being knocked — and their order was not broken.
sentences.i: And all at once came a knock at the door — but it did not throw them off their stride.
sentences.n: إذا of surprise: see the note at the next sentence, where the same construction takes بِـ.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِوَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُمْ انْفَرَدَتْ عَلَى الْبَابِ ثُمَّ عَادَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-wāḥidatin minhum infaradat ʿalā al-bāb thumma ʿādat
sentences.l: and suddenly, there was one of them who went alone to the door, then returned,
sentences.i: and behold, one of them slipped off alone to the door, then came back,
sentences.n: بِـ after إذا of surprise marks what appears (compare وَإِذَا بِغَزَالَةٍ, ‘and behold, a gazelle’); here it is ‘and behold, one of them—’.

sentences.t: وَ قَالَتْ قَدْ كَمَلَ صَفَانَا فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat qad kamala ṣafānā fī tilka al-laylah
sentences.l: and said: ‘Our row is complete for this night.’
sentences.i: and said, ‘We’ve our full number tonight.’
sentences.n: صَفَانَا, literally ‘our row/rank’, i.e. our party, our company.

sentences.t: قَالُوا وَمَا ذَٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: qālū wa-mā dhālika
sentences.l: They said: ‘And what is that?’
sentences.i: ‘What do you mean?’ they asked.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ عَلَى الْبَابِ ثَلٰثَةٌ، أَعْجَامٌ قَرَنْدَلِيَّةٌ، مَحْلُوقِينَ الذُّقُونَ وَالرُّوسَ وَالْحَوَاجِبَ
sentences.tr: qālat ʿalā al-bāb thalāthatun, aʿjāmun qarandaliyyatun, maḥlūqīna al-dhuqūna wa-al-rūsa wa-al-ḥawājib
sentences.l: She said: ‘At the door are three, foreign qalandars, shaven of chin, and head, and eyebrows,
sentences.i: ‘At the door,’ she said, ‘are three foreign qalandars — heads, chins, and brows all shaved,
sentences.n: قرندلية = Qalandars, wandering dervish mendicants who traditionally shave head, beard, and eyebrows. الروس here is a defective spelling of رؤوس (‘heads’), missing its hamza letter, not the unrelated word for ‘Russians’; kept exactly as printed.

sentences.t: وَهُمُ الثَّلٰثَةُ، عُورٌ بِالْعَيْنِ الشِّمَالِ وَهَٰذَا مِنْ أَعْجَبِ الِاتِّفَاقِ
sentences.tr: wa-humu al-thalāthatu, ʿūrun bi-al-ʿayni al-shimāl wa-hādhā min aʿjabi al-ittifāq
sentences.l: and the three of them are one-eyed, in the left eye — and this is among the most wondrous of coincidence.
sentences.i: and all three are blind in the left eye — the strangest coincidence you ever saw.
sentences.n: الشمال (‘the north/left’) used as a noun in place of the adjective ‘left’.

sentences.t: وَهُمْ كَمَا قَدْ حَضَرُوا مِنَ السَّفَرِ الْآنَ وَحَالَةُ السَّفَرِ ظَاهِرَةٌ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-hum kamā qad ḥaḍarū min al-safari al-āna wa-ḥālatu al-safari ẓāhiratun ʿalayhim
sentences.l: and they are as though they have just now come from travel, and the state of travel is visible upon them,
sentences.i: and they look for all the world as if they have just come off the road — travel written all over them,

sentences.t: وَقَدْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ وَهَٰذَا أَوَّلُ دُخُولِهِمْ بَلَدَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad waṣalū ilā Baghdād wa-hādhā awwalu dukhūlihim baladanā
sentences.l: and they have arrived at Baghdad, and this is the first of their entering our city,
sentences.i: and they’ve only just reached Baghdad — this is the very first time they’ve set foot in our city,

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا سَبَبُ دَقِّ الْبَابِ فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمْ يَجِدُوا مَوْضِعًا يَبَاتُوا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā sababu daqqi al-bābi fa-innahum lam yajidū mawḍiʿan yabātū fīhi
sentences.l: As for the reason for the knocking on the door, it is that they did not find a place to spend the night in,
sentences.i: As for why they knocked, they’d found nowhere to lay their heads for the night,
sentences.n: يباتوا (and نبات below) use a colloquial-shaped stem of the verb ‘to spend the night’ rather than the classical hollow-verb forms يبيتوا/نبيت; kept as printed throughout this passage.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا عَسَى صَاحِبَ هَٰذِهِ الدَّارِ يُعْطِينَا مِفْتَاحَ الْإِسْطَبْلِ أَوْ خَرَابَةً، نَبَاتَ فِيهَا اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū ʿasā ṣāḥiba hādhihi al-dāri yuʿṭīnā miftāḥa al-isṭabli aw kharābatan, nabāta fīhā al-laylah
sentences.l: So they said: ‘Perhaps the owner of this house will give us the key of the stable, or a ruin, [that] we may spend the night in it tonight.’
sentences.i: So they said, ‘Perhaps the owner of this house will lend us the key to the stable — or some ruin — where we might spend tonight.’

sentences.t: فَقَلْ أَدْرَكَهُمُ الْمَسَا وَهُمْ غُرَبَاءُ مَا يَعْرِفُونَ أَحَدًا يَلْتَجِئُونَ إِلَيْهِ،
sentences.tr: fa-qal adrakahum al-masā wa-hum ghurabāʾu mā yaʿrifūna aḥadan yaltajiʾūna ilayhi
sentences.l: for — evening had overtaken them, and they are strangers, who know no one to whom they might turn.
sentences.i: for evening had caught them out, and they are strangers who know no one to turn to.
sentences.n: The archive prints فقل here; this is almost certainly a compositor’s slip for فقد (‘for indeed’), the sense followed above. The consonants are kept exactly as printed. المسا is likewise a defective spelling of المساء (‘evening’), missing its final hamza letter; kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَيَا إِخْوَتِي لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ شَكْلٌ وَ صُورَةٌ مُضْحِكَةٌ،
sentences.tr: wa-yā ikhwatī li-kulli wāḥidin minhum shaklun wa-ṣūratun muḍḥikatun
sentences.l: And, O my brothers, each one of them has a shape and an appearance that is funny.
sentences.i: And, my friends, each of them is a sight to make you laugh.
sentences.n: ‘O my brothers’ (يا إخوتي) is a generic, formulaic address here, though the speaker is talking to fellow women — kept as printed rather than read as ‘my sisters’.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَتَلَطَّفُ بِهِمْ حَتَّى قَالُوا لَهَا دَعِيهِمْ يَدْخُلُوا وَ اشْتَرِطِي عَلَيْهِمْ لَا يَتَكَلَّمُوا فِيمَا لَا يَعْنِيهِمْ فَيَسْمَعُوا مَا لَا يُرْضِيهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lam tazal tatalaṭṭafu bihim ḥattā qālū lahā daʿīhim yadkhulū wa-ishtariṭī ʿalayhim lā yatakallamū fīmā lā yaʿnīhim fa-yasmaʿū mā lā yurḍīhim
sentences.l: And she kept gently coaxing them, until they said to her: ‘Let them come in, and make it a condition upon them that they not speak of what does not concern them, lest they hear what does not please them.’
sentences.i: So she kept working on them gently, until they said to her, ‘Let them in, then — but make them agree not to speak of what doesn’t concern them, or they’ll hear what they won’t like.’
sentences.n: بهم and قالوا refer to the same group: she coaxes her companions, who then grant leave; دعيهم and اشترطي are feminine imperatives, addressed to the one who went to answer the door.

sentences.t: فَرِحَتْ وَرَاحَتْ ثُمَّ عَادَتْ وَمَعَهَا الثَّلٰثَةُ، عُورٌ مُحَلَّقِينَ الذَّقَنَ وَ الشَّوَارِبَ
sentences.tr: fariḥat wa-rāḥat thumma ʿādat wa-maʿahā al-thalāthatu, ʿūrun muḥallaqīna al-dhaqana wa-al-shawāriba
sentences.l: She rejoiced, and went, and then came back, with her the three — one-eyed, [their] chin and mustaches shaved,
sentences.i: She was overjoyed, went off, and soon returned with the three of them — one-eyed men, chin and mustache shaved clean,
sentences.n: The subject throughout is the doorkeeper (al-bawwāba), continuing from the sentence before, where the sisters gave her leave to admit the three qalandars on the household's usual condition. 'Having shaved' (muḥallaqīn) governs 'the chin and mustaches' as a direct object rather than the expected construct (muḥallaqī al-dhaqan) — a Middle Arabic looseness kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّمُوا وَخَدَمُوا وَتَأَخَّرُوا فَقَامُوا لَهُمُ الْبَنَاتُ وَرَحَّبُوا وَهَنَّأُوا بِالسَّلَامَةِ وَقَعَّدُوهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-sallamū wa-khadamū wa-taʾakhkharū fa-qāmū lahumu al-banātu wa-raḥḥabū wa-hannaʾū bi-al-salāmati wa-qaʿʿadūhum
sentences.l: So they greeted, and paid respect, and held back; and the girls rose for them, and welcomed [them], and wished [them] joy of safety, and seated them,
sentences.i: The three greeted them, showed their respect, and hung back modestly; the girls rose for them, welcomed them, wished them joy of their safe arrival, and seated them,
sentences.n: 'Rose' (qāmū) is masculine plural though its subject is the girls (al-banāt) — the same loose agreement recurs through this scene, where a feminine group regularly takes masculine-plural verbs.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرُوا الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةُ إِلَى مَحَلٍّ ظَرِيفٍ وَمَقَامٍ نَظِيفٍ مَنْظُومٍ بِخُضْرَةٍ وَشُمُوعٍ تُوقَدُ وَبَخُورٍ تَصَاعَدَ وَنُقْلٍ وَفَوَاكِهَ وَمُدَامٍ وَثَلٰثِ بَنَاتٍ أَبْكَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarū al-qarandaliyyatu ilā maḥallin ẓarīfin wa-maqāmin naẓīfin manẓūmin bi-khuḍratin wa-shumūʿin tūqadu wa-bakhūrin taṣāʿada wa-nuqlin wa-fawākiha wa-mudāmin wa-thalāthi banātin abkārin
sentences.l: And the qalandars looked upon a pleasant place, and a clean abode, arranged with greenery, and candles alight, and incense rising, and sweetmeats, and fruits, and wine, and three maiden girls,
sentences.i: The qalandars looked around at a lovely room, a clean and gracious place set with greenery, candles burning, incense curling upward, sweetmeats, fruit, and wine, and three young unmarried women,
sentences.n: 'Sweetmeats' (nuql) is the stock term for the dried fruit and nuts served alongside wine at a drinking party, not 'transfer', its more everyday sense.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا جَمِيعُهُمْ وَاللَّهِ طَيِّبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū jamīʿuhum wa-allāhi ṭayyibun
sentences.l: And they all said, 'By God, [it is] good.'
sentences.i: And with one voice they all exclaimed, 'By God, how fine!'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتُوا إِلَى الْحَمَّالِ فَوَجَدُوهُ جَذْلَانَ تَعْبَانَ سَكْرَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafatū ilā al-ḥammāli fa-wajadūhu jadhlāna taʿbāna sakrāna
sentences.l: Then they turned to the porter, and found him merry, weary, drunk,
sentences.i: Then they turned to look at the porter, and found him merry, worn out, and drunk,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَايَنُوهُ ظَنُّوا أَنَّهُ مِنْهُمْ وَقَالُوا هُوَ قَرَنْدَلِيٌّ مِثْلُنَا وَهُوَ غَرِيبٌ أَوْ عَرَبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿāyanūhu ẓannū annahu minhum wa-qālū huwa qarandaliyyun mithlunā wa-huwa gharībun aw ʿarabun
sentences.l: And when they saw him, they supposed that he was of them, and said, 'He is a qalandar like us, whether he be a foreigner or an Arab.'
sentences.i: When they set eyes on him they took him for one of their own, and said, 'He's a qalandar like us — whether he's a foreigner or an Arab.'
sentences.n: 'Foreigner' (gharīb) here carries its narrow sense of non-Arab, ʿajamī — the qalandars themselves were introduced earlier as ʿajam, so the porter's origin is genuinely in doubt to them.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْحَمَّالُ هٰذِهِ الْكَلَامَ قَامَ وَحَمْلَقَ عَيْنَيْهِ لَهُمْ وَقَالَ لَهُمُ اقْعُدُوا بِلَا فُضُولٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-ḥammālu hādhihi al-kalāma qāma wa-ḥamlaqa ʿaynayhi lahum wa-qāla lahumu iqʿudū bilā fuḍūlin
sentences.l: And when the porter heard this talk, he rose, and glared his eyes at them, and said to them, 'Sit down, without meddling.'
sentences.i: When the porter heard this talk, he sprang up, glared at them, and said, 'Sit down, and mind your own business.'
sentences.n: 'This' (hādhihi) is feminine though 'the talk' (al-kalām) is masculine — a gender mismatch kept as printed rather than silently corrected.

sentences.t: أَمَّا قَرَأْتُمْ مَا عَلَى الْبَابِ وَمَا بِالْفُقَرَاءِ أَنْتُمْ كَمَا وَرَدْتُمْ عَلَيْنَا تُطْلِقُوا لِسَانَكُمْ فِينَا
sentences.tr: ammā qaraʾtum mā ʿalā al-bābi wa-mā bi-al-fuqarāʾi antum kamā waradtum ʿalaynā tuṭliqū lisānakum fīnā
sentences.l: Have you not read what is on the door? And what [is it] to you dervishes — no sooner had you arrived among us than you loose your tongue at us.
sentences.i: 'Haven't you read what's posted on the door? What business is it of you dervishes — you've barely set foot among us, and already your tongues are running at us?'
sentences.n: The verb 'you loose' (tuṭliqū) is printed without its expected final نَ (tuṭliqūna) — the indicative nūn regularly drops in this copy's verb forms.

sentences.t: قَالُوا نَحْنُ نَقُولُ نَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ يَا فَقِيرُ رَأْسُنَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ
sentences.tr: qālū naḥnu naqūlu nastaghfiru allāha yā faqīru raʾsunā bayna yadayka
sentences.l: They said, 'We — we say, we ask God's forgiveness, O dervish; our head is between your hands.'
sentences.i: They said, 'We — we take it back, we ask God's pardon, good dervish; we put ourselves entirely at your mercy.'
sentences.n: 'Our head is between your hands' is a set idiom of submission — 'do with us as you will' — not meant literally.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكُوا الْبَنَاتُ وَقَامُوا أَصْلَحُوا بَيْنَ الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةِ وَالْحَمَّالِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥikū al-banātu wa-qāmū aṣlaḥū bayna al-qarandaliyyati wa-al-ḥammāli
sentences.l: And the girls laughed, and rose [and] made peace between the qalandars and the porter,
sentences.i: The girls laughed, then got up and made peace between the qalandars and the porter,

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمُوا لِلْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةِ الْأَكْلَ فَأَكَلُوا
sentences.tr: wa-qaddamū lil-qarandaliyyati al-akla fa-akalū
sentences.l: and they set food before the qalandars, and they ate.
sentences.i: and set food before the qalandars, who ate.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسُوا يَتَنَادَمُونَ وَالْبَوَّابَةُ تَسْقِيهِمْ وَدَارَ الْكَاسُ بَيْنَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma jalasū yatanādamūna wa-al-bawwābatu tasqīhim wa-dāra al-kāsu baynahum
sentences.l: Then they sat drinking together as companions, with the doorkeeper serving them drink, and the cup went round among them,
sentences.i: Then they all sat down to drink as companions, the doorkeeper pouring for them, the cup passing round the circle,

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ لِلْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةِ وَأَنْتُمْ يَا أَخَوَاتِنَا مَا مَعَكُمْ حِكَايَةٌ أَوْ نَادِرَةٌ تَحْكُوهَا لَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu lil-qarandaliyyati wa-antum yā akhawātinā mā maʿakum ḥikāyatun aw nādiratun taḥkūhā lanā
sentences.l: The porter said to the qalandars, 'And you, O our sisters, have you no tale or curious story to tell us?'
sentences.i: The porter turned to the qalandars and said, 'And you, my dear sisters — have you no story or strange tale to tell us?'
sentences.n: 'Our sisters' (akhawātinā) is a feminine form of address used in jest: the qalandars, shaved clean of beard and mustache, are teased through this scene as if they were women.

sentences.t: فَلَبِثَتْ عِنْدَهُمُ الْحَرَارَةُ وَطَلَبُوا آلَاتِ اللَّهْوِ فَأَحْضَرَتْ لَهُمُ الْبَوَّابَةُ دُفًّا وَعُودًا وَجَنْكًا أَعْجَمِيًّا
sentences.tr: fa-labithat ʿindahumu al-ḥarāratu wa-ṭalabū ālāti al-lahwi fa-aḥḍarat lahumu al-bawwābatu duffan wa-ʿūdan wa-jankan aʿjamiyyan
sentences.l: And the warmth lingered with them, and they called for instruments of pleasure, and the doorkeeper brought them a tambourine, a lute, and a foreign harp,
sentences.i: The wine's warmth stayed with them, and they called for instruments to make music, so the doorkeeper brought them a tambourine, a lute, and a Persian harp,
sentences.n: 'The warmth' (al-ḥarāra) is the glow of wine still on them, not literal heat; the jank is a Persian harp-like instrument, the 'chang'.

sentences.t: فَقَامُوا الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةُ فَأَصْلَحُوا الْآلَاتِ وَأَخَذَ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمُ الدُّفَّ وَالْآخَرُ الْعُودَ وَالْآخَرُ الْجَنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmū al-qarandaliyyatu fa-aṣlaḥū al-ālāti wa-akhadha wāḥidun minhumu al-duffa wa-al-ākharu al-ʿūda wa-al-ākharu al-janka
sentences.l: And the qalandars rose, and set the instruments in order, and one of them took the tambourine, and another the lute, and another the harp,
sentences.i: The qalandars got up and tuned the instruments — one took the tambourine, another the lute, another the harp,

sentences.t: وَضَرَبُوا بِهَا وَغَنَّوْا وَ الْبَنَاتُ صَرَخَتْ حَتَّى صَارَ لَهُمْ حِسٌّ عَالٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ḍarabū bihā wa-ghannaw wa-al-banātu ṣarakhat ḥattā ṣāra lahum ḥissun ʿālin
sentences.l: and they played them, and sang, and the girls cried out, until they had a loud clamor,
sentences.i: and struck up a tune, and sang, while the girls cried out with them, until the noise rose loud,
sentences.n: 'Played them' (ḍarabū bihā) — ḍaraba bi-, 'to play (an instrument)', literally 'strike with'.

sentences.t: فَهُمْ كَذٰلِكَ وَإِذَا بِالْبَابِ يُطْرَقُ فَقَامَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ تُبْصِرُ خَبَرَ الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-hum kadhālika wa-idhā bi-al-bābi yuṭraqu fa-qāmati al-bawwābatu tubṣiru khabara al-bābi
sentences.l: And while they were thus, behold, there came a knocking at the door; so the doorkeeper rose to see [what was] the matter of the door,
sentences.i: While they were so occupied, suddenly there came a knock at the door, and the doorkeeper got up to see who it was,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ شَهْرَزَادُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ
sentences.tr: qālat Shahrazādu ayyuhā al-maliku
sentences.l: Shahrazad said, 'O King —'

sentences.t: وَكَانَ السَّبَبُ لِدَقِّ الْبَابِ أَنَّ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ نَزَلَ الْخَلِيفَةُ هَارُونُ الرَّشِيدُ بِتَفَرُّجٍ وَيَسْمَعُ مَا يَتَجَدَّدُ مِنَ الْأَخْبَارِ هُوَ وَجَعْفَرٌ وَزِيرُهُ وَمَسْرُورٌ سَيَّافُ نِقْمَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-sababu li-daqqi al-bābi anna tilka al-laylata nazala al-khalīfatu Hārūnu al-Rashīdu bi-tafarrujin wa-yasmaʿu mā yatajaddadu mina al-akhbāri huwa wa-Jaʿfarun wazīruhu wa-Masrūrun sayyāfu niqmatihi
sentences.l: And the reason for the knocking at the door was that on that night the Caliph Harun al-Rashid had gone down [into the city] to look about, and to hear whatever news might arise — he, and Jafar his vizier, and Masrur, the headsman of his vengeance,
sentences.i: The reason for the knock at the door was that the Caliph Harun al-Rashid had gone out into the city that very night to see the sights and pick up whatever news was stirring, together with his vizier Jafar and Masrur, the executioner of his displeasure,
sentences.n: 'The headsman of his vengeance' (sayyāf niqmatihi) is Masrur's stock title in the Nights — the Caliph's executioner, summoned whenever Harun al-Rashid's anger demands a swift death.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ مِنْ عَادَتِهِ يَتَنَكَّرُ فِي صِفَةِ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna min ʿādatihi yatanakkaru fī ṣifati al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And it was of his custom [that] he would disguise himself in the guise of the merchants,
sentences.i: It was his habit to go about disguised as a merchant,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَزَلَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَشَقَّ الْمَدِينَةَ جَاءَتْ طَرِيقُهُمْ عَلَى تِلْكَ الدَّارِ فَسَمِعُوا الْآلَاتِ وَالْغِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā nazala tilka al-laylata wa-shaqqa al-madīnata jāʾat ṭarīquhum ʿalā tilka al-dāri fa-samiʿū al-ālāti wa-al-ghinā
sentences.l: So when he went down that night and crossed the city, their way came upon that house, and they heard the instruments and the singing,
sentences.i: So that night, as he made his way down through the city, their path brought them past that very house, and they heard music and singing,
sentences.n: 'The singing' (al-ghinā) is spelled here without the Classical final hamza (al-ghināʾ) — one more of this copy's regular hamza-dropping spellings.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ لِجَعْفَرٍ أَشْتَهِي أَنْ نَدْخُلَ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الدَّارِ وَنَسْمَعَ هٰذِهِ الْأَصْوَاتَ وَنَرَى أَصْحَابَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-khalīfatu li-Jaʿfarin ashtahī an nadkhula ilā hādhihi al-dāri wa-nasmaʿa hādhihi al-aṣwāta wa-narā aṣḥābahā
sentences.l: The Caliph said to Jafar, 'I desire that we enter this house, and hear these voices, and see its people.'
sentences.i: The Caliph said to Jafar, 'I have a mind for us to go into this house, listen to these voices, and see who is there.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ جَعْفَرٌ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ هٰؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ قَدْ دَخَلَ السُّكْرُ فِيهِمْ وَنَخْشَى أَنْ يُصِيبَنَا مِنْهُمْ شَرٌّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Jaʿfarun yā amīra al-muʾminīna hāʾulāʾi qawmun qad dakhala al-sukru fīhim wa-nakhshā an yuṣībanā minhum sharrun
sentences.l: Jafar said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, these are a people into whom drunkenness has entered, and we fear that some harm may befall us from them.'
sentences.i: Jafar said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, these people are far gone in drink, and I'm afraid some harm might come to us from them.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَابُدَّ مِنْ دُخُولِي وَأُرِيدُكَ أَنْ تَحْتَالَ حَتَّى نَدْخُلَ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā budda min dukhūlī wa-urīduka an taḥtāla ḥattā nadkhula ʿalayhim
sentences.l: He said, 'There is no escaping my entering, and I want you to contrive [a way] so that we may go in upon them.'
sentences.i: He said, 'I must go in, no matter what — I want you to find some ruse to get us inside.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ جَعْفَرٌ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Jaʿfarun samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: Jafar said, '[With] hearing and obedience.'
sentences.i: Jafar said, 'With hearing and obedience.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ جَعْفَرٌ وَطَرَقَ الْبَابَ فَخَرَجَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ وَفَتَحَتِ الْبَابَ
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama Jaʿfarun wa-ṭaraqa al-bāba fa-kharajati al-bawwābatu wa-fataḥati al-bāba
sentences.l: Then Jafar came forward, and knocked at the door; and the doorkeeper came out and opened the door,
sentences.i: Jafar stepped up and knocked, and the doorkeeper came out and opened the door,

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ جَعْفَرٌ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَقَالَ يَا سِتِّي نَحْنُ نَاسٌ تُجَّارٌ مِنْ طَبَرِيَّهْ وَلَنَا فِي بَغْدَادَ عَشَرَةُ أَيَّامٍ وَبِعْنَا تِجَارَتَنَا وَنَحْنُ نَازِلِينَ فِي خَانِ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama Jaʿfarun wa-qabbala al-arḍa wa-qāla yā sittī naḥnu nāsun tujjārun min Ṭabariyyah wa-lanā fī Baghdāda ʿasharatu ayyāmin wa-biʿnā tijāratanā wa-naḥnu nāzilīna fī khāni al-tujjāri
sentences.l: So Jafar came forward, and kissed the ground, and said, 'O my lady, we are people, merchants, from Tiberias, and we have been in Baghdad ten days, and we sold our merchandise, and we are lodging in the merchants' caravanserai,'
sentences.i: Jafar stepped forward, kissed the ground, and said, 'My good lady, we are merchants from Tiberias. We've been ten days in Baghdad, and having sold our goods, we're staying at the merchants' inn,'
sentences.n: The archive spells Tiberias (Ṭabariyya) with a final هـ rather than Classical ة, one of this copy's frequent ة/هـ interchanges; the name is left undeclined. 'Lodging' (nāzilīn) is accusative though it stands as the predicate of a nominal sentence with naḥnu — Classical grammar would want the nominative nāzilūn; kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَعَزَمَ عَلَيْنَا تَاجِرٌ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ فَدَخَلْنَا عِنْدَهُ وَقَدَّمَ لَنَا طَعَامًا فَأَكَلْنَا ثُمَّ تَنَادَمْنَا عِنْدَهُ سَاعَةً فَأَذِنَ لَنَا بِالِانْصِرَافِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿazama ʿalaynā tājirun fī hādhihi al-laylati fa-dakhalnā ʿindahu wa-qaddama lanā ṭaʿāman fa-akalnā thumma tanādamnā ʿindahu sāʿatan fa-adhina lanā bi-al-inṣirāfi
sentences.l: and a merchant invited us this night, so we went in to him, and he set food before us, and we ate; then we sat together as companions with him a while, and he gave us leave to depart,
sentences.i: and a merchant invited us to his house tonight; we went, he set a meal before us and we ate, and afterward we sat with him a while over drinks, until he gave us leave to go,

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْنَا بِاللَّيْلِ وَنَحْنُ غُرَبَاءُ فَتُهْنَا عَنِ الْخَانِ الَّذِي نَحْنُ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajnā bi-al-layli wa-naḥnu ghurabāʾu fa-tuhnā ʿani al-khāni alladhī naḥnu fīhi
sentences.l: and we went out by night, and we being strangers, we lost our way from the caravanserai we are lodged in,
sentences.i: and we set out in the dark and, being strangers here, lost our way back to the inn where we're staying,

sentences.t: فَلَعَلَّ مِنْ صَدَقَاتِكُمْ أَنْ تُدْخِلُونَا هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ عِنْدَكُمْ نَبَاتُ وَلَكُمُ الثَّوَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-laʿalla min ṣadaqātikum an tudkhilūnā hādhihi al-laylata ʿindakum nabātu wa-lakumu al-thawābu
sentences.l: so perhaps, of your charity, you might let us in with you tonight — we spend the night, and yours be the reward,
sentences.i: so, out of your charity, perhaps you'd let us in for the night — you would have our thanks, and God's reward besides,
sentences.n: 'We spend the night' (nabātu) is set beside the verb before it with no connective — 'let us in, [that] we may spend the night' — and itself follows this copy's own colloquial conjugation of bāta, spelled throughout with alif rather than Classical yāʾ (yabītu).

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ إِلَيْهِمْ وَهُمْ مُتَقَمِّشِينَ كَالتُّجَّارِ وَعَلَيْهِمُ الْحَشْمَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarati al-bawwābatu ilayhim wa-hum mutaqammishīna ka-al-tujjāri wa-ʿalayhimu al-ḥashmatu
sentences.l: So the doorkeeper looked at them, they being decked out like merchants, with dignity upon them,
sentences.i: The doorkeeper looked them over — dressed like merchants, and carrying themselves with such dignity,
sentences.n: 'Decked out' (mutaqammishīn) is from qumāsh, 'cloth, goods' — got up in fine merchants' dress, not merely 'clothed.'

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتْ لِإِخْوَتِهَا وَقَالَتْ بِحَدِيثِ جَعْفَرٍ وَتَأَسَّفُوا عَلَيْهِمْ وَقَالُوا لَهَا دَعِيهِمْ يَدْخُلُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalat li-ikhwatihā wa-qālat bi-ḥadīthi Jaʿfarin wa-taʾassafū ʿalayhim wa-qālū lahā daʿīhim yadkhulūna
sentences.l: So she went in to her sisters, and told [them] Jafar's account; and they were moved with pity for them, and said to her, 'Let them come in,'
sentences.i: She went in to her sisters and told them what Jafar had said; they felt for the strangers and said, 'Let them in,'
sentences.n: 'Her sisters' (ikhwatihā) uses the collective noun conventionally meaning 'brothers, brethren' for what are, in context, her fellow sisters in the house — the same loose masculine marking for a female group seen in the verbs throughout this scene.

sentences.t: فَرَدَّتْ وَفَتَحَتْ لَهُمُ الْبَابَ فَقَالُوا لَهَا نَدْخُلُ بِإِذْنِكِ قَالَتِ ادْخُلُوا
sentences.tr: fa-raddat wa-fataḥat lahumu al-bāba fa-qālū lahā nadkhulu bi-idhniki qālati udkhulū
sentences.l: So she went back, and opened the door for them; and they said to her, 'We enter by your leave'; she said, 'Enter,'
sentences.i: So she went back and opened the door for them. 'We come in with your leave,' they said. 'Come in,' she answered,

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ الْخَلِيفَةُ وَجَعْفَرٌ وَمَسْرُورٌ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala al-khalīfatu wa-Jaʿfarun wa-Masrūrun
sentences.l: So the Caliph entered, and Jafar, and Masrur,
sentences.i: So the Caliph went in, with Jafar and Masrur,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْهُمُ الْبَنَاتُ قَامُوا لَهُمْ وَأَجْلَسُوهُمْ وَخَدَمُوهُمْ وَقَالُوا مَرْحَبًا وَأَهْلًا بِالضُّيُوفِ وَلَنَا عَلَيْكُمْ شَرْطٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawhumu al-banātu qāmū lahum wa-ajlasūhum wa-khadamūhum wa-qālū marḥaban wa-ahlan bi-al-ḍuyūfi wa-lanā ʿalaykum sharṭun
sentences.l: And when the girls saw them, they rose for them, and seated them, and served them, and said, 'Welcome, and greetings to the guests; and we have a condition upon you,'
sentences.i: When the girls saw them, they rose to greet them, seated them, and waited on them, saying, 'Welcome, welcome, our guests — though we do have one condition for you,'
sentences.n: Once again the verbs for the girls' actions — 'rose', 'seated', 'served', 'said' — are masculine plural, this copy's regular pattern for a feminine group, not corrected here.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا وَمَا هُوَ قَالُوا لَا تَتَكَلَّمُوا فِيمَا لَا يَعْنِيكُمْ تَسْمَعُوا مَا لَا يَرْضِيكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū wa-mā huwa qālū lā tatakallamū fīmā lā yaʿnīkum tasmaʿū mā lā yarḍīkum
sentences.l: And they said, 'And what is it?' They said, 'Do not speak of what does not concern you, [or] you will hear what does not please you,'
sentences.i: 'And what might that be?' they asked. 'Don't speak of what doesn't concern you,' the girls said, 'or you'll hear what you won't like,'
sentences.n: The condition is stated for the third time in this scene, word for word — first posted on the door, then read aloud by the porter, and now given afresh to each new set of guests.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū naʿam
sentences.l: And they said, 'Yes.'
sentences.i: 'Agreed,' they said.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنَّهُمْ جَلَسُوا لِلشَّرَابِ وَالْمُنَادَمَةِ فَنَظَرَ الْخَلِيفَةُ إِلَى الثَّلٰثَةِ الْقَرَنْلِيَّةِ فَوَجَدَهُمْ عُورًا بِالْعَيْنِ الشِّمَالِ
sentences.tr: thumma annahum jalasū li-al-sharāb wa-al-munādama fa-naẓara al-khalīfa ilā al-thalātha al-qaranliyya fa-wajadahum ʿūran bi-al-ʿayn al-shimāl
sentences.l: Then they sat down to drink and converse, and the Caliph looked at the three qalandars and found them one-eyed in the left eye,
sentences.i: Then they all sat down to drink and talk, and the Caliph studied the three qalandars and saw that each was blind in the left eye,
sentences.n: The archive spells this word al-qaranliyya (القرنلية); the expected word is qalandariyya, 'qalandars' (wandering mendicant dervishes) — likely a compositor's transposition of letters. Left as printed; the same spelling recurs below.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى الْبَنَاتِ وَمَا هُمْ فِيهِ مِنَ الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ فَتَحَيَّرَ وَتَعَجَّبَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba min dhālika wa-naẓara ilā al-banāt wa-mā hum fīhi min al-ḥusn wa-al-jamāl fa-taḥayyara wa-taʿajjaba
sentences.l: He marveled at that, and looked at the girls and at the beauty and loveliness that were in them; and he was bewildered and marveled.
sentences.i: He marveled at the sight, then turned to look the girls over — such beauty and loveliness they had — and was left utterly bewildered.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذُوا فِي الْمُنَادَمَةِ وَ الْحَدِيثِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhū fī al-munādama wa-al-ḥadīth
sentences.l: And they took to conviviality and conversation.
sentences.i: And they fell to drinking and talk together.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لِلْخَلِيفَةِ اشْرَبْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū li-al-khalīfa ishrab
sentences.l: Then they said to the caliph, 'Drink!'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَنَا عَازِمٌ عَلَى الْحَجِّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla anā ʿāzim ʿalā al-ḥajj
sentences.l: He said, 'I am resolved upon the pilgrimage.'

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ وَقَدَّمَتْ سُفْرَةً مُزَرْكَشَةً وَأَقْعَدَتْ عَلَيْهَا بَاطِيَةً صِينِيَّةً وَقَلَبَتْ فِيهَا مَاءَ خِلَافٍ وَأَدْخَلَتْ فِيهَا جُمْحَةَ ثَلْجٍ وَأَبْلُوجَ سُكَّرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat al-bawwāba wa-qaddamat sufra muzarkasha wa-aqʿadat ʿalayhā bāṭiya ṣīniyya wa-qalabat fīhā māʾ khilāf wa-adkhalat fīhā jumḥat thalj wa-ablūj sukkar
sentences.l: Then the doorkeeper rose and set out an embroidered dining-cloth, and placed on it a china bowl, and poured into it willow-flower water, and put into it a lump of ice and a loaf of sugar.
sentences.i: The doorkeeper got up, spread an embroidered cloth, and set on it a porcelain bowl; into it she poured scented willow-water, then dropped in a chunk of ice and a cone of sugar.
sentences.n: māʾ khilāf is willow-flower water, a classical scented drink-water (not plain water). ablūj ('sugar-loaf') is an obscure loanword whose exact vocalization is conjectural; it is treated here as having its own hamza (a-) by default rather than as one of the small set of words that drop it, since it does not belong to any of those patterns.

sentences.t: فَشَكَرَهَا الْخَلِيفَةُ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَاللَّهِ لَأَجْزِيهَا فِي غَدَاةِ غَدٍ عَلَى فِعْلِهَا مِنَ الْخَيْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-shakarahā al-khalīfa wa-qāla fī nafsihi wa-Allāhi la-ajzīhā fī ghadāti ghad ʿalā fiʿlihā min al-khayr
sentences.l: The caliph thanked her, and said to himself, 'By God, I shall surely reward her, on the morrow of tomorrow, for what she did of good.'
sentences.i: The caliph thanked her, and said to himself, 'By God, tomorrow morning I will repay her for this kindness.'
sentences.n: ghadāt ghad ('the morrow of tomorrow') is simply an emphatic way of saying 'tomorrow morning.' After an oath (wa-Allāhi) with lām, Classical grammar expects the energetic mood (la-ajziyannahā); the archive's la-ajzīhā is a simpler, non-classical construction, left as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اشْتَغَلُوا بِمُنَادَمَتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: thumma ishtaghalū bi-munādamatihim
sentences.l: Then they busied themselves with their conviviality.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَحَكَّمَ الشَّرَابُ قَامَتِ السِّتُّ وَخَدَمَتْهُمْ وَأَخَذَتْ بِيَدِ الْخَشْكَاشَةِ وَقَالَتْ يَا أُخْتِي قُومِي نَقْضِي دَيْنَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taḥakkama al-sharāb qāmat al-sitt wa-khadamathum wa-akhadhat bi-yad al-khushkāsha wa-qālat yā ukhtī qūmī naqḍī dīnanā
sentences.l: When the wine took hold, the lady rose and served them, and took Khushkasha by the hand, and said, 'O my sister, get up — let us discharge our due.'
sentences.i: Once the wine had taken hold of them, the lady of the house rose to serve them, then took Khushkasha by the hand and said, 'Come, sister — time to do our part.'
sentences.n: 'Our due' (dīnanā, lit. 'our debt') is figurative here: a ritual obligation the sisters perform for every gathering, not a literal debt. Khushkasha functions as a name or epithet for one of the two sisters, not an ordinary common noun; its origin is uncertain.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْأُخْتَانِ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat al-ukhtān naʿam
sentences.l: The two sisters said, 'Yes.'

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ قَامَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ قُدَّامَهُمْ وَذٰلِكَ بَعْدَ أَنْ عَزَلَتِ الْمَقَامَ وَرَمَتِ الْقُشُورَ وَغَيَّرَتِ الْبَخُورَ وَعَزَلَتْ وَسَطَ الْقَاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāmat al-bawwāba quddāmahum wa-dhālika baʿda an ʿazalat al-maqām wa-ramat al-qushūr wa-ghayyarat al-bakhūr wa-ʿazalat wasaṭ al-qāʿa
sentences.l: At that, the doorkeeper rose before them; and that was after she had cleared away the sitting-place, thrown out the peelings, changed the incense, and cleared the middle of the hall.
sentences.i: At this, the doorkeeper rose and stood before them — she had already cleared the table, swept away the fruit-peelings, freshened the incense, and cleared the center of the hall.
sentences.n: al-maqām here means the dining-setting/sitting-place that had been in use, not a shrine or station in the later, more familiar sense of the word.

sentences.t: وَأَطْلَعَتِ الْقَرَنْلِيَّةَ إِلَى جَانِبِ الْإِيوَانِ عَلَى صُفَّةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-aṭlaʿat al-qaranliyya ilā jānib al-īwān ʿalā ṣuffa
sentences.l: And she brought the qalandars up to the side of the iwan, onto a raised bench.
sentences.i: She led the three qalandars off to one side of the hall, to a bench by the iwan.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتِ الْخَلِيفَةَ وَجَعْفَرًا وَمَسْرُورًا إِلَى جَانِبِ الْقَصْرِ عَلَى صُفَّةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhat al-khalīfa wa-Jaʿfaran wa-Masrūran ilā jānib al-qaṣr ʿalā ṣuffa
sentences.l: And she took the caliph, Jaʿfar, and Masrūr to the side of the alcove, onto a bench.
sentences.i: She brought the caliph, Jaʿfar, and Masrūr over to the other side, to a bench by the alcove.
sentences.n: al-qaṣr here is an architectural term for a recessed alcove or inner chamber, paired symmetrically with al-īwān in the previous sentence — not 'palace' in the ordinary sense.

sentences.t: وَصَرَخَتْ عَلَى الْحَمَّالِ وَقَالَتْ مَا قَلَّ مَوَدَّتُكَ أَنْتَ مَا أَنْتَ غَرِيبٌ أَنْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الدَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣarakhat ʿalā al-ḥammāl wa-qālat mā qalla mawaddatuka anta mā anta gharīb anta min ahl al-dār
sentences.l: And she cried out at the porter and said, 'How little is your affection! You — you are no stranger, you are one of the people of the house.'
sentences.i: She called sharply to the porter: 'What little regard you show us! Come now — you are no stranger here, you are one of the household.'
sentences.n: The archive's qalla mawaddatuka lacks both the feminine verb-ending expected if mawadda is its subject (qallat) and the hamza of the usual exclamatory pattern (mā aqalla, 'how little!'). Read here as an idiomatic reproach rather than repointed to the classical exclamatory form.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْحَمَّالُ وَشَدَّ وَسَطَهُ وَ قَالَ مَا تُرِيدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-ḥammāl wa-shadda wasaṭahu wa-qāla mā turīdī
sentences.l: The porter rose, girded his waist, and said, 'What do you want?'
sentences.i: The porter got to his feet, tightened his belt, and asked, 'What would you have of me?'
sentences.n: turīdī drops the classical final -na of the feminine imperfect (turīdīna); a colloquial form, addressed to the woman who has just spoken to him.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ قِفْ مَكَانَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat qif makānaka
sentences.l: She said, 'Stand in your place.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتِ الْخَشْكَاشَةُ وَنَصَبَتْ فِي وَسَطِ الْقَاعَهِ كُرْسِيًّا
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat al-khushkāsha wa-naṣabat fī wasaṭ al-qāʿa kursiyyan
sentences.l: Then Khushkasha rose and set up, in the middle of the hall, a chair.
sentences.i: Then Khushkasha got up and placed a chair in the middle of the hall.
sentences.n: The archive spells al-qāʿa with hā' here rather than the tā' marbūṭa used elsewhere in this passage — almost certainly a typesetting substitution of the visually similar letter, not a different word; read and vocalized the same way, as al-qāʿa, 'the hall.'

sentences.t: وَفَتَحَتْ خُوشْكَانَةً وَقَالَتْ لِلْحَمَّالِ سَاعِدْنِي
sentences.tr: wa-fataḥat khūshkānatan wa-qālat li-al-ḥammāl sāʿidnī
sentences.l: And she opened a khūshkāna, and said to the porter, 'Help me.'
sentences.i: She opened a little store-closet and said to the porter, 'Give me a hand.'
sentences.n: khūshkāna is obscure, likely a Persian loan (khushk, 'dry') for a closet or cabinet used to store dry goods; its precise sense is uncertain and the vocalization here is conjectural.

sentences.t: فَرَأَى كَلْبَتَيْنِ سُودًا فِي رِقَابِهِمْ جَنَازِيرُ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾā kalbatayn sūdan fī riqābihim janāzīr
sentences.l: Then he saw two bitches, black, chains in their necks.
sentences.i: There he saw two black bitches, chains around their necks.
sentences.n: sūdan ('black') and riqābihim ('their necks,' masc. plural) do not formally agree with the dual kalbatayn ('two she-dogs'); the archive treats the pair with plural rather than dual agreement throughout this passage, a common leveling in Middle Arabic. Left as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِلْحَمَّالِ خُذْهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat li-al-ḥammāl khudhhum
sentences.l: She said to the porter, 'Take them.'

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهُمُ الْحَمَّالُ وَخَرَجَ بِهِمْ إِلَى وَسَطِ الْقَاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahum al-ḥammāl wa-kharaja bihim ilā wasaṭ al-qāʿa
sentences.l: The porter took them and went out with them to the middle of the hall.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ صَاحِبَةُ الْمَنْزِلِ وَشَمَّرَتْ عَنْ مِعْصَمِهَا وَأَخَذَتْ سَوْطًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat al-ṣabiyya ṣāḥibat al-manzil wa-shammarat ʿan miʿṣamihā wa-akhadhat sawṭan
sentences.l: Then the young woman, the mistress of the house, rose, bared her wrist, and took up a whip.
sentences.i: The young mistress of the house then rose, rolled back her sleeve, and picked up a whip.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِلْحَمَّالِ قَدِّمْ كَلْبَةً مِنْهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat li-al-ḥammāl qaddim kalbatan minhum
sentences.l: And she said to the porter, 'Bring forward one of them, a she-dog.'
sentences.i: She told the porter, 'Bring one of them forward.'

sentences.t: فَقَدَّمَهَا وَجَرَّهَا فِي الْجِنْزِيرِ وَالْكَلْبَةُ تَبْكِي وَتَحَرَّكَتْ رَأْسُهَا إِلَى الصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qaddamahā wa-jarrahā fī al-jinzīr wa-al-kalba tabkī wa-taḥarrakat raʾsuhā ilā al-ṣabiyya
sentences.l: He brought her forward and dragged her by the chain, while the bitch was weeping, and her head turned toward the young woman.
sentences.i: He led her forward, dragging her by the chain, while the poor creature wept, her head turning toward the young woman.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ عَلَيْهَا بِالضَّرْبِ عَلَى رَأْسِهَا وَالْكَلْبَةُ تَصْرُخُ وَلَا زَالَتْ تَضْرِبُهَا حِينَ كَلَّتْ سَوَاعِدُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-nazalat al-ṣabiyya ʿalayhā bi-al-ḍarb ʿalā raʾsihā wa-al-kalba taṣrukh wa-lā zālat taḍribuhā ḥīna kallat sawāʿiduhā
sentences.l: Then the young woman came down upon her with blows, on her head, while the bitch screamed; and she did not stop beating her until her arms grew weary.
sentences.i: The young woman fell upon her, raining blows on her head, while the poor bitch shrieked — and she did not stop beating her until her arms gave out from exhaustion.

sentences.t: فَرَمَتِ السَّوْطَ مِنْ يَدِهَا وَضَمَّتِ الْكَلْبَةَ لِصَدْرِهَا وَمَسَحَتْ دُمُوعَ الْكَلْبَةِ بِيَدِهَا وَبَاسَتْ رَأْسَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ramat al-sawṭ min yadihā wa-ḍammat al-kalba li-ṣadrihā wa-masaḥat dumūʿ al-kalba bi-yadihā wa-bāsat raʾsahā
sentences.l: Then she threw the whip from her hand, clasped the bitch to her breast, wiped the bitch's tears with her hand, and kissed her head.
sentences.i: Then she flung the whip from her hand, gathered the bitch to her breast, wiped away her tears, and kissed her on the head.
sentences.n: bāsat ('kissed') is the colloquial verb bāsa/yabūs rather than Classical qabbala; left as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلْحَمَّالِ خُذِيهَا وَهَاتِ الثَّانِيَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-ḥammāl khudhīhā wa-hāti al-thāniya
sentences.l: Then she said to the porter, 'Take her! And bring the second.'
sentences.i: Then she said to the porter, 'Take her away, and bring the other one.'
sentences.n: khudhīhā is a feminine imperative ('take her!'), though addressed to al-ḥammāl (masc.) — an inconsistency in the archive, not corrected here.

sentences.t: فَجَابَهَا وَفَعَلَتْ بِهَا مِثْلَ مَا فَعَلَتْ بِالْأُولَى
sentences.tr: fa-jābahā wa-faʿalat bihā mithla mā faʿalat bi-al-ūlā
sentences.l: He brought her, and she did with her as she had done with the first.
sentences.i: He brought her over, and she did to her just as she had done to the first.
sentences.n: jābahā is the colloquial contraction of jāʾa bihā ('he brought her'), not the Classical verb; kept as archived.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ اشْتَغَلَ قَلْبُ الْخَلِيفَةِ وَضَاقَ صَدْرُهُ وَعَيِيَ صَبْرُهُ لِيَعْرِفَ خَبَرَ هٰذَيْنِ الْكَلْبَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ishtaghala qalb al-khalīfa wa-ḍāqa ṣadruhu wa-ʿayiya ṣabruhu li-yaʿrifa khabar hādhayn al-kalbayn
sentences.l: At that, the caliph's heart grew troubled, his breast tightened, and his patience failed him, that he might know the story of these two bitches.
sentences.i: At this the caliph's heart grew heavy, his chest tightened, and his patience gave out — he was desperate to learn the story of these two bitches.

sentences.t: فَغَمَزَ جَعْفَرً فَالْتَفَتَ لَهُ وَقَالَ بِالْإِشَارَةِ اُسْكُتْ
sentences.tr: fa-ghamaza Jaʿfar fa-iltafata lahu wa-qāla bi-al-ishāra uskut
sentences.l: Then he signaled to Jaʿfar; he turned to him and said, by gesture, 'Be silent!'
sentences.i: The caliph signaled to Jaʿfar, who turned toward him and, with a gesture, said: 'Not a word!'
sentences.n: The archive spells the accusative Jaʿfar here without the customary alif of tanwīn (jaʿfaran), unlike wa-jaʿfaran earlier in this passage; likely a compositor's omission, left as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ لِلْبَوَّابَةِ فَقَالَتْ لَهَا قُومِي اِقْضِي مَا عَلَيْكِي فَقَالَتْ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafatat al-ṣabiyya li-al-bawwāba fa-qālat lahā qūmī iqḍī mā ʿalaykī fa-qālat naʿam
sentences.l: Then the young woman turned to the doorkeeper, and said to her, 'Get up, discharge what is upon you.' She said, 'Yes.'
sentences.i: Then the young woman turned to the doorkeeper and said, 'Up now — pay what you owe.' 'Yes,' she said.
sentences.n: ʿalaykī carries an extra final -ī beyond the classical second-feminine-singular suffix -ki (ʿalayki); a colloquial lengthening, left as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا قَامَتْ وَصَعِدَتْ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ وَهُوَ مِنَ الْعَرْعَرِ مُصَفَّحٌ بِصَفَايِحِ الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā qāmat wa-ṣaʿidat ʿalā al-sarīr wa-huwa min al-ʿarʿar muṣaffaḥ bi-ṣafāyiḥ al-dhahab wa-al-fiḍḍa
sentences.l: Then indeed she rose and mounted the couch, which was of juniper-wood, plated with plates of gold and silver.
sentences.i: Then she rose and climbed onto the couch — it was made of juniper wood, sheathed in plates of gold and silver.
sentences.n: The archive spells ṣafāyiḥ ('plates,' plural of ṣafīḥa) with a plain yāʾ where Classical orthography places the medial hamza on a yāʾ seat (ṣafāʾiḥ) — a common period typesetting convention. Left as printed and read the same way.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلْبَوَّابَةِ وَالْخَشْكَاشَةِ هَاتُوا مَا عِنْدَكُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-bawwāba wa-al-khushkāsha hātū mā ʿindakum
sentences.l: Then she said to the doorkeeper and Khushkasha, 'Bring what you have.'
sentences.i: Then she said to the doorkeeper and Khushkasha, 'Bring out what you have.'
sentences.n: hātū is masculine/common plural, though addressed to two women — another instance of the loose gender and number agreement running through this scene.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيٍّ بِجَانِبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat wa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyin bi-jānibihā
sentences.l: So she rose and sat on a chair beside her.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْخَشْكَاشَةُ فَإِنَّهَا دَخَلَتْ مَخْدَعًا وَ خَرَجَتْ وَمَعَهَا كِيسُ أَطْلَسَ بِشَرَارِيطَ خُضْرٍ وَبِشَمْعَتَيْنِ ذَهَبٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-khushkāsha fa-innahā dakhalat makhdaʿan wa-kharajat wa-maʿahā kīs aṭlas bi-sharārīṭ khuḍr wa-bi-shamʿatayn dhahab
sentences.l: As for Khushkasha, she went into an alcove, and came out with her a satin bag with green ribbons, and with two gold candlesticks.
sentences.i: As for Khushkasha, she withdrew into an alcove and came back out carrying a satin bag trimmed with green ribbons, along with two gold candlesticks.

sentences.t: وَ وَقَفَتْ قُدَّامَ الصَّبِيَّةِ صَاحِبَةِ الْمَنْزِلِ وَنَقَضَتِ الْكِيسَ فَأَخْرَجَتْ مِنْهُ عُودَ غِنَاءٍ
sentences.tr: wa-waqafat quddām al-ṣabiyya ṣāḥibat al-manzil wa-naqaḍat al-kīs fa-akhrajat minhu ʿūd ghināʾ
sentences.l: And she stood before the young woman, the mistress of the house, and untied the bag, and took out of it a lute of song.
sentences.i: She stood before the young mistress of the house, untied the bag, and drew out from it a lute.

sentences.t: فَأَصْلَحَتْ أَوْتَارَهُ وَشَدَّتْ مَلَاوِيَهُ وَأَصْلَحَتْهُ إِصْلَاحًا جَيِّدًا
sentences.tr: fa-aṣlaḥat awtārahu wa-shaddat malāwiyahu wa-aṣlaḥathu iṣlāḥan jayyidan
sentences.l: Then she set its strings right, tightened its pegs, and put it in good order, a good putting-in-order.
sentences.i: She tuned its strings, tightened the pegs, and set it in perfect order.
sentences.n: iṣlāḥan jayyidan ('a good setting-right') is a cognate-accusative intensifier; rendered idiomatically as 'in perfect order.'

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāt
sentences.l: And she began to recite, saying these verses:
sentences.i: And she struck up a song, reciting these lines:

sentences.t:
اَنْتُمْ مُرَادِي وَقَصْدِي * ووَصلُكُم يَا اَحِبَّتي
فِيهِ النَّعِيمُ الدَّايِمُ * وَالْبُعْدُ عَنْكُمْ نَارُ
بِكُمْ جُنُونِي وَفِيكُمْ * تَوَلُّهِي طُولَ الزَّمَانْ
وَمَا عَلَيَّ اِذَا مَا * اَحْبَبْتُكُمْ مِنْ عَارْ
تَهَتَّكَتْ اَسْتَارِي * لَمَّا انْشَغَفْتُ بِكُمْ
وَالْحُبُّ مَازَالَ يَهْتِكْ * وَيَفْضَحُ الاَسْتَارْ
ثَوبُ الضَّنا قَدْ لَبِسته * فَبَانَ عُذْرِي وَاتَّضَحْ
مِنْ اَجْلِ ذَا فِي غَرَامِي * قَلْبِي بِكُمْ يَخْتَارْ
جَرَتْ دُمُوعِي تَجْرِي * فَبَانَ سِرِّي وَاشْتَهَرْ
ضِيَا جُفُونِكَ ضَنًى لِي * قَتْلِي بِسَيْفِ صَبَابَتِي
وَكَمْ بِسَيْفِ الْمَحَبَّةِ * قَدْ مَاتَتِ الاَخْيَارِ
لَا اَنْتَهِي عَنْ غَرَامِي * وَ لَا اَنِيلُ لِسَلْوَتِي
قَالِبُ طَبِّي شَرِعِي * زِينَى فِي السِّرِّ وَ الِاجْهَارِ
يَا سَعِدَ عَيْنٍ تَمَلَّتْ * مِنْكُمْ وَ فَازَتَ بِالنَّظَرِ
نَعَمْ وَ قَدْ عَارَ قَامِي * مَوْلَهَا مُخْتَارَ
sentences.tr:
antum murādī wa-qaṣdī * wa-waṣlukum yā aḥibbatī
fīhi al-naʿīmu al-dāyimu * wa-al-buʿdu ʿankum nāru
bikum junūnī wa-fīkum * tawalluhī ṭūla al-zamān
wa-mā ʿalayya idhā mā * aḥbabtukum min ʿār
tahattakat astārī * lammā inshaghaftu bikum
wa-al-ḥubbu mā zāla yahtik * wa-yafḍaḥu al-astār
thawbu al-ḍanā qad labisteh * fa-bāna ʿudhrī wa-ittaḍaḥ
min ajli dhā fī gharāmī * qalbī bikum yakhtār
jarat dumūʿī tajrī * fa-bāna sirrī wa-ishtahar
ḍiyā jufūnika ḍanan lī * qatlī bi-sayfi ṣabābatī
wa-kam bi-sayfi al-maḥabbati * qad mātati al-akhyāri
lā antahī ʿan gharāmī * wa-lā anīlu li-salwatī
qālibu ṭabbī sharʿī * zīnā fī al-sirri wa-al-ijhār
yā saʿida ʿaynin tamallat * minkum wa-fāzat bi-al-naẓar
naʿam wa-qad ʿāra qāmī * mawlahā mukhtāra
sentences.l:
You are my whole desire and my aim; and union with you, O my beloveds,
in it is everlasting bliss; and to be far from you is fire.
Through you is my madness, and in you my rapt-devotion, the whole length of time.
And what disgrace is upon me, if I have loved you?
My veils were torn away, when I became enraptured with you,
for love has not ceased to tear away and expose the veils.
The garment of love-sickness I have worn, so my excuse stood plain and clear.
For that, in my passion, my heart chooses you.
My tears flowed, kept flowing, so my secret became apparent and known.
The brightness of your eyelids is a sickness to me; my slaying is by the sword of my ardent-love.
And how many, by the sword of love, have died already — the good, the choicest of men!
I do not desist from my passion, nor do I attain to my consolation.
The mould of my cure is my own law: my beauty(?), in secret and in the open.
O the good fortune of an eye that took its fill of you, and won its prize through the sight of you!
Yes, and indeed my stature has grown bent — hers, her chosen one(?).
sentences.i:
You are my whole desire, my only aim; and to be joined with you, my dear ones,
is everlasting bliss — while to be far from you is fire itself.
Through you I am driven mad, and in you my heart's devotion lives on for as long as time shall run.
And what disgrace is it to me, that I have loved you?
Every veil of mine was torn away, once I fell captive to your spell,
for love never tires of tearing away and laying bare the veils.
I have worn the very garment of love-sickness, until my excuse for it stood plain for all to see.
For that, in my passion, it is you my heart chooses above all others.
My tears ran and kept running, until my secret came out and was known to everyone.
The brightness of your eyes is itself a sickness to me; I am slain by the very sword of my longing.
And how many good souls, before me, have died by that same sword of love!
I will not give up my passion, nor will I ever come to any comfort.
My cure follows no law but my own: your beauty, alike in secret and in the open.
Oh, how fortunate the eye that gazed its fill of you, and won its prize in the very seeing of you!
Yes — my very stature has grown bent with longing — I am hers, her chosen one, to command.
sentences.n: Two lines resist confident translation and are flagged rather than smoothed over. قَالِبُ طَبِّي شَرِعِي زِينَى فِي السِّرِّ وَالِاجْهَارِ (line 13) is rendered by sense — ‘my cure follows my own law; your beauty, alike in secret and in the open’ — but زِينَى, printed with a final alif maqṣūra, is read here as a colloquial contraction of زِينَتِي, ‘my/your beauty, adornment,’ rather than corrected to that fuller spelling. In the last line, نَعَمْ وَقَدْ عَارَ قَامِي مَوْلَهَا مُخْتَارَ, عَارَ (from a root spelled ع-و-ر, ‘to be defective, to fail’) is read as ‘became bent/wasted’ — the stock image of a lover's stature worn down by longing — and the poem's abrupt close, ‘hers, her chosen one,’ is left as compressed as the Arabic leaves it. Several other spellings are kept exactly as the edition points them though a stricter Classical hand would differ: الدَّايِمُ for دَائِمُ, اَنِيلُ for the expected أَنَالُ, and the case ending of الاَخْيَارِ (printed with kasra where the sense wants the nominative الْأَخْيَارُ, subject of مَاتَتْ).

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ ذَٰلِكَ الْقَصِيدَ الرُّبَاعِيَّ قَالَتْ اَهْ اَهْ اَهْ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā samiʿati al-ṣabiyyatu dhālika al-qaṣīda al-rubāʿiyya qālat ah ah ah
sentences.l: He said: Then, when the girl heard that quatrain, she said, ‘Ah! Ah! Ah!’
sentences.i: He said: Now when the girl heard that quatrain-poem, she cried out, ‘Ah! Ah! Ah!’
sentences.n: الْقَصِيد الرُّبَاعِيّ, ‘the poem in quatrains,’ names the piece of verse just heard — a form built of paired, rhyming stanzas, as the poem above shows. اَهْ is printed here without the cry’s usual hamza-and-madda spelling (آه); it is read as a short, clipped exclamation of pain.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَقَّتْ أَثْوَابَهَا وَوَقَعَتْ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ مُغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma shaqqat athwābahā wa-waqaʿat ʿalā al-arḍi mughshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: Then she tore her garments and fell to the ground, swooned-upon (in a swoon).
sentences.i: Then she tore her clothes and fell to the ground in a dead faint.

sentences.t: فَرَأَى الْخَلِيفَةُ ضَرْبَ الْمَقَارِعِ وَالْكَسَّارَاتِ فَتَعَجَّبَ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾā al-khalīfatu ḍarba al-maqāriʿi wa-al-kassārāti fa-taʿajjaba ghāyata al-ʿajab
sentences.l: Then the Caliph saw the marks of the scourges and the rods, and he wondered the utmost of wonder.
sentences.i: Then the Caliph saw the marks the whips and rods had left on her, and he was utterly astonished.
sentences.n: الْمَقَارِع and الْكَسَّارَات, 'scourges' and 'rods/breakers,' point back to a beating this girl suffered earlier in the story, offstage; what the Caliph actually sees here are its marks on her.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ وَرَشَّتِ الْمَاءَ عَلَيْهَا وَأَتَتْ لَهَا بِبِدْلَةٍ سَنِيَّةٍ وَأَلْبَسَتْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāmati al-bawwābatu wa-rashshati al-māʾa ʿalayhā wa-atat lahā bi-bidlatin saniyyatin wa-albasathā
sentences.l: So the doorkeeper rose and sprinkled the water upon her, and brought her a splendid change of clothes, and dressed her in it.
sentences.i: So the doorkeeper got up and sprinkled water over her, brought her a fine change of clothes, and dressed her in it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَايَنُوا الْجَمَاعَةُ ذَٰلِكَ تَكَدَّرَ خَاطِرُهُمْ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا الْقِصَّةَ وَلَا الْخَبَرَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿāyanū al-jamāʿatu dhālika takaddara khāṭiruhum wa-lam yaʿlamū al-qiṣṣata wa-lā al-khabar
sentences.l: Then when they — the company — witnessed that, their mind grew troubled, and they did not know the story nor the news.
sentences.i: When the company saw this happen, they were all thrown into confusion, for they knew neither the story nor the reason behind it.
sentences.n: عَايَنُوا الْجَمَاعَةُ puts the verb first with its plural pronoun ending (‘they witnessed’), then names the subject afterward (‘the company’) — a common Middle Arabic word order, not the Classical rule that a fem. or plural noun-subject following its verb takes a singular verb.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَٰلِكَ قَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ لِجَعْفَرَ مَا تَنْظُرُ إِلَى هَٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَكَيْفَ عَلَيْهَا وَهَٰذَا الضَّرْبُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāla al-khalīfatu li-Jaʿfara mā tanẓuru ilā hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati wa-kayfa ʿalayhā wa-hādhā al-ḍarb
sentences.l: Then at that, the Caliph said to Jaʿfar: Do you not look at this girl, and how it is upon her, and this beating?
sentences.i: At that, the Caliph said to Jaʿfar: Do you not see this girl — the state she is in, and this beating she has taken?
sentences.n: مَا تَنْظُرُ is read as a rhetorical question (‘do you not see’) rather than a flat negative, matching the Caliph’s exclamation of astonishment.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا لَا أَنْدُرُ أَسْكُتَ إِلَّا أَنْ وَقَفْتُ عَلَى حَقِيقَةِ الْحَالِ وَخَبَرِ هَٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَخَبَرِ الْكَلْبَتَيْنِ السُّودِ
sentences.tr: fa-anā lā anduru askuta illā an waqaftu ʿalā ḥaqīqati al-ḥāli wa-khabari hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati wa-khabari al-kalbatayni al-sūd
sentences.l: For I do not — slip? — [that] I be silent, except that I stand upon the truth of the state, and the news of this girl, and the news of the two black she-dogs.
sentences.i: For I cannot bear to stay silent until I get to the bottom of this — the truth of this girl’s story, and the story of the two black bitches.
sentences.n: أَنْدُرُ is printed exactly so; at face value it is a form of نَدَرَ, ‘to be rare, to slip out,’ which gives no good sense here. It is translated by context, as a stand-in for ‘I cannot manage/bear to,’ but the reading is a guess and the letters are kept as printed rather than silently corrected to, say, أَقْدِرُ. السُّود, ‘black’ (m. pl.), modifies the dual الْكَلْبَتَيْنِ — a plural adjective on a dual noun, again not the Classical agreement rule.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ جَعْفَرُ يَا مَوْلَانَا قَدْ شَرَطُوا عَلَيْنَا أَنَّنَا لَمْ نَتَكَلَّمْ فِيمَا لَا يَعْنِينَا فَنَسْمَعَ مَا لَا يُرْضِينَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Jaʿfaru yā mawlānā qad sharaṭū ʿalaynā annanā lam natakallam fīmā lā yaʿnīnā fa-nasmaʿa mā lā yurḍīnā
sentences.l: Then Jaʿfar said: O our master, they have already set a condition upon us that we not speak of what does not concern us, lest we hear what does not please us.
sentences.i: Then Jaʿfar said: My lord, we were made to agree, before we ever came in, that we would not speak of what is none of our business — or we should hear what we would not like to hear.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ بِاللَّهِ يَا أُخْتِي أَوْفِينِي وَ اتِيني
sentences.tr: thumma qālat bi-Allāhi yā ukhtī awfīnī wa-ītīnī
sentences.l: Then she said: By God, my sister, make good to me, and come to me.
sentences.i: Then she said, ‘By God, my sister, keep your word to me — come now!’
sentences.n: اتيني is printed with none of the letters that would normally mark the radical hamza of أَتَى, ‘to come’ (a fuller spelling would be ائتيني); it is read here as that same imperative, come to me, with the hamza elided in speech and in the spelling alike, as this edition often does.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْخُوشْكَاشَةُ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً وَأَخَذَتِ الْعُودَ وَأَسْنَدَتْهُ إِلَى نَهْدَيْهَا وَجَسَّتْهُ بِأَنَامِلِهَا وَأَنْشَلَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-Khūshkāshatu ḥubban wa-karāmatan wa-akhadhati al-ʿūda wa-asnadathu ilā nahdayhā wa-jassathu bi-anāmilihā wa-anshalat taqūl
sentences.l: Then Khushkasha said, ‘Gladly and with honor,’ and took the lute, and rested it against her two breasts, and touched it with her fingertips, and began, saying:
sentences.i: Then Khushkasha said, ‘Gladly, with all my heart,’ and took up the lute, propped it against her breast, ran her fingertips over it, and struck up, saying:
sentences.n: الْخُوشْكَاشَة is kept as printed, a name or byname not found in ordinary dictionaries — most likely, on its consonants, a Turkish-flavoured nickname (khosh, ‘pleasing’) for this companion, rather than any common noun. وَأَنْشَلَتْ literally reads as a form of نَشَلَ, ‘to snatch up, pull out’ — but the whole scene is the Nights’ standing formula for striking up a song, elsewhere spelled أَنْشَدَتْ / أَنْشَأَتْ تَقُولُ (‘she began, reciting’), and it is translated on that understanding while the printed letters are left exactly as they stand.

sentences.t:
اِنْ شَكَوْنَا بُعْداً فَمَا ذَا نَقُـولُ * اَوْ بَلَغْنَا شَوْقاً فَاَيْنَ السَّبِيلُ
اَوْ بَعَثْنَا رُسُلاً تَتَرْجِمُ عَنَّا * مَا يُودِي شَكْوَى الْمُحِبّ رَسُولُ
اَوْ صَبَرْنَا فَمَا بَقِيَ الْمُحِبُّ * بَعْدَ فَقْدِ الْاَحْبَابِ اِلَّا قَلِيلُ
لَيْسَ اِلَّا تَاَسُّفًا تَمَّ حُزْنَا * وَ دُمُوعاً عَلَى الْخُدُودِ تَسِيلُ
اَيُّهَا الْغَائِبِينَ عَنْ شَخْصِ عَيْنِي * وَ هُمْ فِي الْفُؤَادِ مِنِّي حُلُولُ
اَ تَرَاكُمْ فَهَلْ عَلِمْتُمْ بِعَهْدِي * فَهُوَ طُولُ الْمَاءِ لَيْسَ يَطُولُ
اَمْ تَنَاسَيْتُمْ عَلَى الْعَبْدِ صَبّاً * يَشْتَفِي فِيكُمُ الْبُكَا وَ النُّحُولُ
آهِ اِنْ ضَمَّنَا وَ اِيَّاكُمُ الْحُبُّ * فَلِي مَعَكُمْ عِتَابٌ يَطُولُ
sentences.tr:
in shakawnā buʿdan fa-mā dhā naqūlu * aw balaghnā shawqan fa-ayna al-sabīlu
aw baʿathnā rusulan tatarjimu ʿannā * mā yūdī shakwā al-muḥibb rasūlu
aw ṣabarnā fa-mā baqiya al-muḥibbu * baʿda faqdi al-aḥbābi illā qalīlu
laysa illā taʾassufan tamma ḥuznā * wa-dumūʿan ʿalā al-khudūdi tasīlu
ayyuhā al-ghāʾibīna ʿan shakhṣi ʿaynī * wa-hum fī al-fuʾādi minnī ḥulūlu
a-tarākum fa-hal ʿalimtum bi-ʿahdī * fa-huwa ṭūlu al-māʾi laysa yaṭūlu
am tanāsaytum ʿalā al-ʿabdi ṣabban * yashtafī fīkumu al-bukā wa-al-nuḥūlu
āhi in ḍammanā wa-iyyākumu al-ḥubbu * fa-lī maʿakum ʿitābun yaṭūlu
sentences.l:
If we complain of separation, then what shall we say? — or if we reach the utmost of longing, then where is the way?
Or we send messengers to speak on our behalf — no messenger carries off the complaint of the lover.
Or we endure patiently — the lover does not remain, after the loss of the loved ones, except a little.
There is nothing but regret, grief brought to its fullness, and tears upon the cheeks, flowing.
O you who are absent from the sight of my eye, while they, in the heart, are dwelling within me.
Do I see you? Have you known of my covenant? — for it, like the length of water, does not last long.
Or have you forgotten a slave, passionately in love, in whom weeping and wasting-away find their cure through you?
Ah, if love should join us and you together — then I have with you a reproach that runs long.
sentences.i:
If we complain of this parting, what is left to say? And if our longing reaches its utmost, where lies the way out?
Or we might send messengers to speak for us — but no messenger can carry the full weight of a lover's complaint.
Or we might simply endure — yet once the beloved is lost, little of the lover himself remains.
There is nothing left but regret, grief brought to its fullness, and tears streaming down the cheeks.
O you who are gone from my sight, and yet you dwell always within my heart.
Do I truly see you? Have you even remembered the bond between us? For it, like flowing water, does not last.
Or have you forgotten a devoted slave of love, whose weeping and wasting away are all for your sake?
Ah, if love should ever join the two of us together, I still have a long reckoning to settle with you.
sentences.n: يُودِي (line 2) is printed exactly so, without the hamza and doubled dāl of the expected يُؤَدِّي, ‘conveys’; read on its actual letters it is rather يُودِي from أَوْدَى, ‘to destroy, carry off’ — so literally ‘no messenger disposes of the lover's complaint,’ which the translation folds into ‘carries off’ to keep both readings in view. طُولُ الْمَاءِ, ‘the length of the water’ (line 6), is obscure; it is taken as a compressed image for something as short-lived as flowing water, but no confident paraphrase is offered beyond that. أَيُّهَا الْغَائِبِينَ (line 5) keeps the accusative-looking ending printed on the vocative noun, where Classical grammar would want the nominative الْغَائِبُونَ.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْقَصِيدَةَ الثَّانِيَةَ صَرَخَتْ وَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ طَيِّبٌ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā samiʿati al-qaṣīdata al-thāniyata ṣarakhat wa-qālat wa-allāhi ṭayyibun
sentences.l: He said: Then when she heard the second qasida, she cried out and said: “By God, that is fine!”
sentences.i: Then, hearing the second poem, she cried out. “By God,” she said, “how lovely!”
sentences.n: The subject here is not named; the next clause ('as the first one had done') marks her as a different sister from the one who swooned at the first poem, and 'the third girl' is named explicitly at the parallel moment after the third poem below — so the three swoons in turn belong to each of the three sisters of the house, though which is which, beyond 'the first', 'this one', and 'the third', is not recoverable from the pronouns alone.

sentences.t: وَ حَطَّتْ يَدَهَا وَشَقَّتْ أَثْوَابَهَا كَمَا فَعَلَتِ الْأُولَى ثُمَّ وَقَعَتْ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaṭṭat yadahā wa-shaqqat athwābahā kamā faʿalati al-ūlā thumma waqaʿat ʿalā al-arḍi maghshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And she put down her hand and tore her garments, as the first one had done, then fell upon the ground, swooned-over.
sentences.i: She clutched at herself and tore her clothes, as the first sister had done, then fell to the ground in a swoon.
sentences.n: حَطَّتْ يَدَهَا ('put her hand down') is left elliptical, as if for a gesture completed by the next clause — probably 'reached for her collar,' matching the fuller حَطَّتْ يَدَهَا فِي أَثْوَابِهَا used of the third sister below. مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا, 'one swooned-over,' is a fixed idiom for fainting: a passive participle frozen in the masculine accusative regardless of the subject's own gender.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الْخَشْكَاشَةُ وَأَلْبَسَتْهَا بِدْلَةً ثَانِيَةً بَعْدَ أَنْ رَشَّتْ عَلَيْهَا الْمَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmati al-khashkāshatu wa-albasathā bidlatan thāniyatan baʿda an rashshat ʿalayhā al-māʾa
sentences.l: Then Khushkasha arose, and dressed her in a second garment, after she had sprinkled the water upon her.
sentences.i: Then Khushkasha got up and put a fresh change of clothes on her, after sprinkling water over her.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ وَجَلَسَتْ ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِأُخْتِهَا الْخَشْكَاشَةِ زِيدِينِي وَ أَوْفِي دَيْنِي فَمَا بَقِيَ غَيْرُ هَذَا الصَّوْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat wa-jalasat thumma qālat li-ukhtihā al-khashkāshati zīdīnī wa-awfī daynī fa-mā baqiya ghayru hādhā al-ṣawti
