sentences.l: Then she rose and sat down; then she said to her sister Khushkasha: “Add more for me, and pay out my due — for nothing remains but this voice.”
sentences.i: She got up and sat down again, then said to her sister Khushkasha, “Give me more, and see my due paid in full — nothing is left now but this voice.”
sentences.n: زِيدِينِي وَأَوْفِي دَيْنِي, 'add to me, and discharge my due,' figures the unfinished song of mourning as a debt still owed her; 'this voice' is the singing itself, the last comfort left to her.

sentences.t: فَأَحْضَرَتِ الْخَشْكَاشَةُ الْعُودَ وَ أَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-aḥḍarati al-khashkāshatu al-ʿūda wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: So Khushkasha brought the lute, and recited, saying these verses, in verse:
sentences.i: So Khushkasha fetched the lute and recited these lines:
sentences.n: Khushkasha is kept as printed, a name or byname not found in ordinary dictionaries, of uncertain origin. وَأَنْشَلَتْ literally reads as a form of نَشَلَ, 'to snatch up, pull out' — but the whole scene is the Nights' standing formula for striking up a song, elsewhere spelled أَنْشَدَتْ / أَنْشَأَتْ تَقُولُ ('she began, reciting'), and it is translated on that understanding while the printed letters are left exactly as they stand.

sentences.t:
حَتّى مَتـى هَذَا الصُّلُودُ وَ ذَا الْجَفَا * اَ فَمَا جَرَى مِنْ اَدْمُعِي مَا قَدْ كَفَا
وَ لَكُمْ تُطِيلُ الْهَجْرَ لِيْ مُتَعَمِّدَا * اِنْ كَانَ قَصْدُكَ حَاسِدِيْ فَقَدِ اشْتَفَى
لَوْ اَنْصَفَ الدَّهْرُ الْخَؤُونُ لِعَاشِقٍ * مَا بَاتَ سَهْراً فِي هَوَاهَا مُدْنَفَا
رِفْقًا عَلَيَّ فَقَدْ اَضَرَّ بِيَ الْجَفَا * يَا مَالِكِيْ مَا آنَ اَنْ تَتَعَطَّفَا
فَلِمَنْ اُبِيحُ صَبَابَتِيْ يَا قَاتِلِيْ * يَا خَيْبَةَ الشَّاكِيْ اِذَا قَلَّ الْوَفَا
وَ يَزِيلُ وَجْدِيْ فِيكُمُ وَ عَبْرَتِيْ * وَ يَطُولُ اَيَّامُ الصُّدُودِ فَيُخْلِفَا
يَا مُسْلِمِيْنَ خُلُّوا بِثَارِ مُتَيَّمٍ * اَلِفَ السُّهَادَ وَ رَبْعُ صَبْرِهِ قَدْ عَفَا
اَ يَحِلُّ فِي شَرْعِ الْهَوَى يَا مُنْيَتِيْ * بَعْلِيْ وَ غَيْرِيْ بِالْوِصَالِ مُشَرَّفَا
وَ لِاَيِّ دَعَةٍ بِالْجِوَارِ تَلَذُّذًا * كَمْ جَهْدَ مَنْ اَهْوَاهُ اَنْ يَتَكَلَّفَا
sentences.tr:
ḥattā matā hādhā al-ṣulūdu wa-dhā al-jafā * a-famā jarā min admuʿī mā qad kafā
wa-lakum tuṭīlu al-hajra lī mutaʿammidā * in kāna qaṣduka ḥāsidī fa-qadi shtafā
law anṣafa al-dahru al-khaʾūnu li-ʿāshiqin * mā bāta sahran fī hawāhā mudnafā
rifqan ʿalayya fa-qad aḍarra biya al-jafā * yā mālikī mā āna an tataʿaṭṭafā
fa-liman ubīḥu ṣabābatī yā qātilī * yā khaybata al-shākī idhā qalla al-wafā
wa-yazīlu wajdī fīkumu wa-ʿabratī * wa-yaṭūlu ayyāmu al-ṣudūdi fa-yukhlifā
yā muslimīna khullū bi-thāri mutayyamin * alifa al-suhāda wa-rabʿu ṣabrihi qad ʿafā
a-yaḥillu fī sharʿi al-hawā yā munyatī * baʿlī wa-ghayrī bi-al-wiṣāli musharrafā
wa-li-ayyi daʿatin bi-al-jiwāri talādhdhudhan * kam jahda man ahwāhu an yatakallafā
sentences.l:
Until when [shall there be] this coldness and this harshness? * Has what has flowed from my tears not already sufficed?
And to you (falls) the prolonging of estrangement against me, deliberately; * if your intent was [to please] my envier, he has indeed been gratified.
If treacherous Time dealt justly with a lover, * he would not spend the night sleepless, love-sick for her.
Gentleness upon me! For cruelty has harmed me. * O my master, has the time not come for you to relent?
To whom, then, shall I lay open my passion, O my killer? * O, the disappointment of the complainer, when faithfulness runs short!
And my passion for you (pl.) and my tears do not vanish, * and the days of estrangement grow long, until he breaks (his word).
O Muslims, leave [me] to the vengeance of a love-smitten one, * grown used to sleeplessness, the abode of whose patience has become effaced.
Is it lawful, in the law of passion, O my heart's-desire, * that my husband — and one other than I — be honored with union?
And for what ease, in nearness, for the sake of enjoyment — * how much toil has he whom I love undertaken, that he should trouble himself!
sentences.i:
How long, this coldness and this cruelty? * Has the flow of my tears not been enough?
How long, and always by design, you draw out my estrangement! * If it was to please my rival, his envy is well appeased.
Were treacherous Time ever just to a lover, * he would not lie sleepless the whole night, sick with love of her.
Be gentle with me — this cruelty has done me harm! * O my sovereign, is it not time you relented?
To whom, then, shall I bare my passion, O my slayer? * How wretched is the complainer's lot when faith runs thin!
My longing for you and my tears will not fade, * and the days of estrangement stretch on, until faith itself is broken.
O believers, let vengeance fall on this love-struck man, * grown used to sleepless nights, the very seat of his patience now in ruins.
Is it lawful, by love's own law, O my heart's desire, * that my lord — and a rival besides — should be granted the union denied to me?
And what repose is there in nearness, what pleasure to be had, * when the one I love must labor so, just to trouble himself to come near?
sentences.n: This qasida keeps a single rhyme in -afā throughout (kafā, ishtafā, mudnafā, tataʿaṭṭafā, al-wafā, fa-yukhlifā, ʿafā, musharrafā, yatakallafā). Its hamzas are printed, as usual in this edition's verse, as plain alif with a vowel and no hamza sign (اَدْمُعِي for أَدْمُعِي, اُبِيحُ for أُبِيحُ, and so on) — kept exactly as the edition points them; the Khؤون of line 3 (الخَؤُونُ) is the one word in the whole passage the edition does print with the hamza sign. لَكُمْ and فِيكُمُ address the single beloved with an honorific plural, alongside the singular يَا مَالِكِيْ and يَا مُنْيَتِيْ elsewhere in the same poem. بَعْلِيْ in the eighth line is literally 'my husband,' but can equally be 'my lord, my master'; either suits a jealous complaint about a rival granted the beloved's favor. The sixth line's وَيَزِيلُ ... فَيُخْلِفَا leaves its subject unstated, as Middle Arabic verse often does; it is read here as the beloved's doing.

sentences.t: قٰلَ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الثَّالِثَةُ قَصِيدَتَهَا صَرَخَتْ وَحَطَّتْ يَدَهَا فِي أَثْوَابِهَا وَشَقَّتْهَا إِلَى الذَّيْلِ وَوَقَعَتْ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا ثَالِثَ مَرَّةٍ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā samiʿati al-ṣabiyyatu al-thālithatu qaṣīdatahā ṣarakhat wa-ḥaṭṭat yadahā fī athwābihā wa-shaqqathā ilā al-dhayli wa-waqaʿat ʿalā al-arḍi maghshiyyan ʿalayhā thālitha marratin
sentences.l: He said: Then, when the third girl heard her qasida, she screamed, and put her hand into her garments and tore them to the hem, and fell upon the ground, swooned-over, a third time.
sentences.i: Then, when the third girl heard her own poem, she screamed, clutched at her garments and tore them clear to the hem, and fell to the ground in a swoon, for the third time.

sentences.t: فَبَانَ ضَرْبُ الْقَارِعِ فَقَالَتِ الْفَرَنْلِيَّةُ لَيْتَنَا لَمَّا دَخَلْنَا هَذِهِ الدَّارَ وَكُنَّا نِمْنَا عَلَى الْكِيمَانِ فَقَدْ تَعَكَّرَ مُقَامُنَا بِشَيْءٍ يَقْطَعُ الْقَلْبَ
sentences.tr: fa-bāna ḍarbu al-qāriʿi fa-qālati al-faranliyyatu laytanā lammā dakhalnā hādhihi al-dāra wa-kunnā nimnā ʿalā al-kīmāni fa-qad taʿakkara maqāmunā bi-shayʾin yaqṭaʿu al-qalba
sentences.l: Then the stroke of the calamity became apparent, and the qalandars said: “Would that, when we entered this house, we had instead slept upon the rubbish-heaps! For our stay has been troubled by something that cuts the heart.”
sentences.i: It became plain that some calamity had befallen them, and the qalandars said, “Would that, instead of entering this house, we had slept on the rubbish-heaps! Our stay here has been spoiled by something that cuts to the heart.”
sentences.n: ضَرْبُ الْقَارِعِ, literally 'the blow of the striker,' is obscure; it is kept exactly as printed and read here as an idiom for a sign of calamity becoming visible (compare الْقَارِعَة, 'the Calamity,' the Qur'anic name for Judgment Day). الْفَرَنْلِيَّة is printed only here; the household's three dervish-guests are elsewhere in this passage called الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّة, and this is very probably the same word under another spelling — the edition already varies الْخَشْكَاشَة three ways elsewhere in this tale — so it is translated here as 'the qalandars' like every other occurrence, while the Arabic spelling itself is kept exactly as archived rather than emended.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ الْخَلِيفَةُ إِلَيْهِمْ وَقَالَ لَهُمْ لِمَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata al-khalīfatu ilayhim wa-qāla lahum lima dhālika
sentences.l: Then the Caliph turned to them and said to them: “Why [is] that?”
sentences.i: The Caliph turned to them and asked, “Why is that?”

sentences.t: قَالُوا قَدِ اشْتَغَلَ سِرُّنَا بِهَذَا الْأَمْرِ
sentences.tr: qālū qadi shtaghala sirrunā bi-hādhā al-amri
sentences.l: They said: “Our inner self has become occupied with this matter.”
sentences.i: They said, “Our minds have been troubled by this matter.”
sentences.n: سِرّ, literally 'secret,' stands here for the inner self, the heart or mind — a Sufi-tinged usage fitting for wandering dervishes.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ مَا أَنْتُمْ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَيْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-khalīfatu mā antum min hādhā al-bayti
sentences.l: Then the Caliph said: “You are not of this household.”
sentences.i: The Caliph said, “You are not part of this household.”

sentences.t: قَالُوا لَا وَلَا رَأَيْنَا هَذَا الْمَوْضِعَ إِلَّا فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: qālū lā wa-lā raʾaynā hādhā al-mawḍiʿa illā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: They said: “No — nor have we seen this place, except at this very hour.”
sentences.i: They said, “No — we had never even seen this place before this very hour.”

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ وَقَالَ فَيَكُونُ الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي عِنْدَكُمْ يَعْرِفُ خَبَرَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba wa-qāla fa-yakūnu al-rajulu alladhī ʿindakum yaʿrifu khabarahum
sentences.l: So he marveled, and said: “Then the man who is with you must know their story.”
sentences.i: He marveled at this, and said, “Then it must be the man with you who knows their story.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ غَمَزَ الْحَمَّالَ وَسَأَلَهُ عَنِ الْأَحْوَالِ
sentences.tr: thumma ghamaza al-ḥammāla wa-saʾalahu ʿani al-aḥwāli
sentences.l: Then he signaled to the porter, and asked him about the circumstances.
sentences.i: Then he gave the porter a sign, and questioned him about the affair.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ وَاللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ كُلُّنَا بِالْهَوَى سَوِيٌّ وَأَنَا نَشْوًا بَغْدَادَ وَعُمْرِي مَا دَخَلْتُ هَذِهِ الدَّارَ إِلَّا فِي هَذَا النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu wa-allāhi al-ʿaẓīmi kullunā bi-al-hawā sawiyyun wa-anā nashwan baghdāda wa-ʿumrī mā dakhaltu hādhihi al-dāra illā fī hādhā al-nahāri
sentences.l: The porter said: “By God the Mighty, all of us are alike in passion; and I, by upbringing, [am] of Baghdad, and in my life I never entered this house except on this very day.”
sentences.i: The porter said, “By God almighty, we're all equally strangers here. I'm Baghdad born and bred, and never in my life did I set foot in this house before today.”
sentences.n: نَشْوًا is printed as though from a root ن ش و and is read here as an accusative of specification, 'by upbringing, by origin' — most likely an irregular or softened spelling for نَشَأً, a 'growing-up,' from نَشَأَ, 'to grow up' (compare نَشَأْتُ بِبَغْدَادَ, 'I grew up in Baghdad'); kept exactly as printed rather than emended.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ تَعَادِي عِنْدَهُمْ عَجَبٌ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna taʿādī ʿindahum ʿajabun
sentences.l: And it was — their not knowing one another — in their eyes, a wonder.
sentences.i: And they found it strange, this not knowing each other.
sentences.n: تَعَادِي, evidently the masdar of VI taʿādā, 'to be mutually estranged, unacquainted,' is printed with no case ending the spelling can support (an accusative -an here would need a final alif the text does not have); it is pointed as an invariable form here rather than forcing an ending, as with شِعْرٌ elsewhere in this project's practice.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا وَاللَّهِ حَسِبْنَا أَنَّكَ مِنْهُمْ وَالْآنَ نَرَاكَ نَظِيرَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālū wa-allāhi ḥasibnā annaka minhum wa-al-āna narāka naẓīranā
sentences.l: So they said: “By God, we thought you were one of them — and now we see you [are] our equal.”
sentences.i: They said, “By God, we took you for one of them — but now we see you're just like us.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْخَلِيفَةَ قَالَ نَحْنُ سَبْعَةُ رِجَالٍ وَهُمْ ثَلٰثَةُ نِسَاءٍ لَيْسَ لَهُمْ رَابِعٌ فَاسْأَلُوهُمْ عَنْ حَالِهِمْ فَإِنْ لَمْ يُجِيبُونَا طَوْعًا أَجَابُونَا كَرْهًا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-khalīfata qāla naḥnu sabʿatu rijālin wa-hum thalāthatu nisāʾin laysa lahum rābiʿun fa-isʾalūhum ʿan ḥālihim fa-in lam yujībūnā ṭawʿan ajābūnā karhan
sentences.l: Then, indeed, the Caliph said: “We are seven men, and they are three women; they have no fourth. So ask them about their state; and if they do not answer us willingly, they will answer us under compulsion.”
sentences.i: Then the Caliph spoke up: “We are seven men, and they are three women, short of a fourth. Question them about themselves — if they will not answer us willingly, we shall make them answer whether they like it or not.”

sentences.t: وَاتَّفَقَ الْجَمِيعُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ittafaqa al-jamīʿu ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: And all of them agreed on that.
sentences.i: And they all agreed to it.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ جَعْفَرٌ مَا هَذَا رَأْيٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Jaʿfarun mā hādhā raʾyun
sentences.l: Then Jaafar said: “This is not [sound] opinion.”
sentences.i: Jaafar said, “That is not wise.”

sentences.t: دَعُوهُمْ فَنَحْنُ ضُيُوفٌ عِنْدَهُمْ وَشَرَطُوا عَلَيْنَا شَرْطًا وَقَدْ قَبِلْنَا شَرْطَهُمْ كَمَا عَلِمْتُمْ
sentences.tr: daʿūhum fa-naḥnu ḍuyūfun ʿindahum wa-sharaṭū ʿalaynā sharṭan wa-qad qabilnā sharṭahum kamā ʿalimtum
sentences.l: Leave them be, for we are guests among them, and they laid upon us a condition, and we have already accepted their condition, as you know.
sentences.i: Leave them be — we are guests in their house. They set us a condition, and we have already accepted it, as you all know.

sentences.t: فَالْأَوْلَى سُكَاتُنَا عَنْ هَذَا الْأَمْرِ وَقَدْ بَقِيَ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ الْقَلِيلُ وَكُلٌّ مِنَّا يَمْضِي إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-al-awlā sukātunā ʿan hādhā al-amri wa-qad baqiya mina al-layli al-qalīlu wa-kullun minnā yamḍī ilā ḥāli sabīlihi
sentences.l: So the more fitting [course] is our silence about this matter; and little of the night remains, and each of us goes on his way.
sentences.i: The wiser course, then, is for us to say nothing more about it. Little of the night is left — let each of us go about his business.
sentences.n: الْأَوْلَى here is the elative 'more fitting, preferable,' not the ordinal 'the first' used of the sisters earlier in the story — the same bare spelling, الاولى, covers both words.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ غَمَزَ الْخَلِيفَةُ وَقَالَ لَهُ مَا بَقِيَ إِلَّا سَاعَةٌ وَفِي غَدٍ نُحْضِرُهُمْ بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ وَتَسْأَلُهُمْ عَنْ قِصَّتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: thumma ghamaza al-khalīfatu wa-qāla lahu mā baqiya illā sāʿatun wa-fī ghadin nuḥḍiruhum bayna yadayka wa-tasʾaluhum ʿan qiṣṣatihim
sentences.l: Then the Caliph signaled, and said to him: “Only an hour remains; and tomorrow we will bring them before you, and you will ask them about their story.”
sentences.i: The Caliph gave him a sign and said, “There is only an hour left. Tomorrow we will bring them before you, and you may question them about their story.”

sentences.t: فَرَفَعَ الْخَلِيفَةُ رَأْسَهُ وَصَرَخَ مُغْضَبًا وَقَالَ مَا بَقِيَ لِي صَبْرٌ عَنْ خَبَرِهِمْ فَلْنَدَعِ الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةَ يَسْأَلُوهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-rafaʿa al-khalīfatu raʾsahu wa-ṣarakha mughḍaban wa-qāla mā baqiya lī ṣabrun ʿan khabarihim fa-l-nadaʿi al-qarandaliyyata yasʾalūhum
sentences.l: Then the Caliph raised his head, and cried out, enraged, and said: “I have no more patience left concerning news of them — so let us leave it to the qalandars; let them ask them.”
sentences.i: The Caliph lifted his head, cried out in anger, and said, “I cannot wait any longer to know their story — let the qalandars question them.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ جَعْفَرٌ مَا هَذَا بِرَأْيٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Jaʿfarun mā hādhā bi-raʾyin
sentences.l: Then Jaafar said: “This is not [any sound] opinion.”
sentences.i: Jaafar said, “That is not wise either.”

sentences.t: فَتَفَاوَضُوا فِي الْكَلَامِ وَكَثُرَ بَيْنَهُمُ الْقَالُ وَالْقِيلُ فِيمَنْ يَسْأَلُهُمْ قَبْلُ
sentences.tr: fa-tafāwaḍū fī al-kalāmi wa-kathura baynahumu al-qālu wa-al-qīlu fīman yasʾaluhum qablu
sentences.l: So they conferred over the matter, and there grew, among them, much saying-and-being-said about who should ask them first.
sentences.i: So they argued the matter back and forth, and there was much wrangling among them over who should question them first.
sentences.n: الْقَالُ وَالْقِيلُ, literally 'the said and the being-said,' is a set doublet for idle talk or wrangling.

sentences.t: قَالُوا الْحَمَّالُ
sentences.tr: qālū al-ḥammālu
sentences.l: They said: “The porter.”
sentences.i: They said, “Let it be the porter.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُمُ الصَّبِيَّةُ يَا جَمَاعَةُ لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ تَفُوشُوا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahumu al-ṣabiyyatu yā jamāʿatu li-ayyi shayʾin tafūshū
sentences.l: Then the girl said to them: “O company, for what thing are you making a fuss?”
sentences.i: Then the girl said to them, “What is all this commotion about, good people?”
sentences.n: تَفُوشُوا is not a Classical form; it is read here as a colloquial verb meaning 'to make a fuss, wrangle noisily' (compare Egyptian Arabic فَوْشَة, 'commotion, uproar'), kept exactly as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْحَمَّالُ لِصَاحِبَةِ الْبَيْتِ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا سِتِّي إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ الْجَمَاعَةَ يُحِبُّونَ أَنْ تُحَدِّثِيهِمْ بِخَبَرِ الْكَلْبَتَيْنِ وَمَا قِصَّتُهُمْ وَ كَيْفَ أَنْتِ تُعَاقِبِيهِمْ وَتَعُودِي تَبْكِي وَتَبُوسُهُمْ وَأَخْبِرْهُمْ عَنْ أُخْتِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-ḥammālu li-ṣāḥibati al-bayti wa-qāla lahā yā sittī inna hāʾulāʾi al-jamāʿata yuḥibbūna an tuḥaddithīhim bi-khabari al-kalbatayni wa-mā qiṣṣatuhum wa-kayfa anti tuʿāqibīhim wa-taʿūdī tabkī wa-tabūsuhum wa-akhbirhum ʿan ukhtiki
sentences.l: Then the porter rose to the mistress of the house, and said to her: “O my lady, these people wish that you tell them the story of the two she-dogs, and what their story is, and how you punish them, and go back to weeping, and kiss them — and tell them about your sister.”
sentences.i: So the porter went up to the mistress of the house and said to her, “My lady, these good people would like you to tell them about the two bitches and what their story is — how it is that you beat them, then fall to weeping and kissing them again — and to tell them about your sister.”
sentences.n: The dropped nūn across تُحَدِّثِي, تُعَاقِبِي and تَعُودِي (Classical تُحَدِّثِينَ, تُعَاقِبِينَ, and so on) is a regular feature of this edition's Middle Arabic 2fs verbs, kept as printed; وَتَبُوسُهُمْ goes a step further and drops the ي itself along with the nūn. وَأَخْبِرْهُمْ breaks the pattern differently: it reads as a plain masculine-form imperative, 'tell them!' — the porter's own interjected request rather than a continuation of the indirect 'they wish that you...' clause; imperatives addressed to a woman keep the masculine form in this register.

sentences.t: وَعَرَضَهَا بِالْمَتَاجِرِ مِثْلَ الرِّجَالِ وَهَٰذَا سِوَارُكُمْ لَكِ وَالسَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿaraḍahā bi-al-matājir mithla al-rijāl wa-hādhā siwārukum laki wa-al-salām
sentences.l: and she offered it in the markets like the men; and this is your bracelet — it is yours — and that is all
sentences.i: and she went and traded it in the markets just as men do — 'and here is your bracelet: it is yours, and that's the whole of it.'
sentences.n: The referent of 'she/it' lies earlier in the story and cannot be recovered here. سواركم ('your', pl.) and لك ('you', f.sg.) do not agree in number; لك may be a compositor's slip for لكم. والسلام here is the idiom 'and that's that, end of story,' not the greeting — unrelated to the famous catchphrase associated with this text.

sentences.t: قَالَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ صَاحِبَةُ الْمَكَانِ لِلضُّيُوفِ صَحِيحٌ مَا يَقُولُ عَنْكُمْ
sentences.tr: qālat al-ṣabiyya ṣāḥibat al-makān li-al-ḍuyūf: ṣaḥīḥun mā yaqūlu ʿankum?
sentences.l: the young woman, mistress of the place, said to the guests: 'true, what he says about you?'
sentences.i: The girl who was mistress of the house asked the guests, 'Is it true, what he says about you?'
sentences.n: The antecedent of 'he' lies earlier in the story and is not recoverable here.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا الْجَمِيعُ نَعَمْ إِلَّا جَعْفَرَ فَإِنَّهُ سَكَتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū al-jamīʿ: naʿam, illā Jaʿfara fa-innahu sakata
sentences.l: and they all said: 'yes' — except Jaʿfar, for he was silent
sentences.i: They all said yes — all but Jaʿfar, who said nothing.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ كَلَامَهُمْ قَالَتْ وَاللَّٰهِ لَقَدْ أٰذَيْتُمُونِي يَا ضُيُوفَنَا الْأَذِيَّةَ الْبَالِغَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat al-ṣabiyya kalāmahum qālat: wa-Allāhi laqad ādhaytumūnī yā ḍuyūfanā al-adhiyyata al-bāligha
sentences.l: and when the young woman heard their words, she said: 'by God, you have indeed hurt me, O our guests, the utmost hurt'
sentences.i: When the girl heard what they said, she cried, 'By God, you have wounded me, my guests — wounded me to the core.'
sentences.n: الأذية البالغة is a cognate accusative intensifying أٰذيتموني: literally 'you have hurt me the utmost hurting.'

sentences.t: وَتَقَدَّمَ لَنَا أَنَّا شَرَطْنَا عَلَيْكُمْ أَنَّ مَنْ تَكَلَّمَ فِيمَا لَا يَعْنِيهِ سَمِعَ مَا لَا يُرْضِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-taqaddama lanā annā sharaṭnā ʿalaykum anna man takallama fīmā lā yaʿnīhi samiʿa mā lā yurḍīhi
sentences.l: and it was already stated to us that we had stipulated upon you that whoever speaks about what does not concern him hears what does not please him
sentences.i: As we told you from the start, we set you one condition: whoever speaks of what is not his concern will hear what he does not like.

sentences.t: وَمَا كَنَاكُمْ أَنَّنَا أَدْخَلْنَاكُمْ مَنْزِلَنَا وَأَطْعَمْنَاكُمْ زَادَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-mā kanākum annanā adkhalnākum manzilanā wa-aṭʿamnākum zādanā?
sentences.l: and was it not enough for you that we admitted you into our house and fed you our provisions?
sentences.i: And was that not enough for you — that we took you into our home and fed you our own food?
sentences.n: The archive prints كناكم, which is not a recognizable Classical Arabic word here; it is most likely a misprint for كفاكم ('was that enough for you'), which is how it is translated. The letters are left exactly as printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا لَكُمْ ذَنْبٌ الذَّنْبُ لِمَنْ أَوْصَلَكُمْ إِلَيْنَا
sentences.tr: wa-mā lakum dhanbun; al-dhanbu li-man awṣalakum ilaynā
sentences.l: and you have no fault; the fault belongs to whoever brought you to us
sentences.i: None of this is your doing — the fault lies with whoever led you to us.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَمَّرَتْ عَنْ مِعْصَمِهَا وَضَرَبَتِ الْأَرْضَ ثَلَٰثَ ضَرَبَاتٍ وَقَالَتْ عَجِّلُوا
sentences.tr: thumma shammarat ʿan miʿṣamihā wa-ḍarabat al-arḍa thalātha ḍarabātin wa-qālat: ʿajjilū
sentences.l: then she bared her wrist, and struck the ground three blows, and said: 'hurry!'
sentences.i: Then she bared her wrist, struck the ground three times, and cried, 'Quickly!'
sentences.n: Striking the ground here is a summoning gesture — it is what brings the armed slaves of the next sentence.

sentences.t: وَ إِذَا بِبَابِ خُرُسْتَانَةٍ قَلْ فُتِحَ وَخَرَجَ مِنْهُ سَبْعُ عَبِيدٍ وَبِأَيْدِيهِمْ سُيُوفٌ مَسْلُولَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-bābi khurustānatin qal futiḥa, wa-kharaja minhu sabʿu ʿabīdin wa-bi-aydīhim suyūfun maslūla
sentences.l: and behold, with a door of a closet — it had been opened — and out of it came seven slaves, with drawn swords in their hands
sentences.i: And suddenly the door of a closet stood open, and out came seven slaves, swords drawn in their hands.
sentences.n: قل does not sit comfortably as قال ('said' — a door cannot speak) or, fully, as the defective spelling of قد either, but 'already/indeed' is by far the more plausible sense, so it is rendered as if قد, though the letters are left exactly as printed. خرستانة is not a Classical word; it appears to be a non-classical/dialectal term for a closet or storeroom. سبع (rather than the Classically expected سبعة before the masculine-counted عبيد) shows the loosened numeral–gender agreement typical of this print.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ كَتِّفُوا هَٰؤُلَاءِ الْكَثِيرِينَ الْكَلَامَ وَارْبِطُوا بَعْضَهُمْ بِبَعْضٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat: kattifū hāʾulāʾi al-kathīrīna al-kalāma, wa-irbiṭū baʿḍahum bi-baʿḍin
sentences.l: and she said: 'bind these many-of-talk ones, and tie some of them to some other'
sentences.i: She said, 'Pinion these chatterboxes, and bind them to one another.'
sentences.n: الكثيرين الكلام is a colloquial turn of phrase — a definite noun followed directly by an accusative of specification, without the case-marking a Classical iḍāfa would need — literally 'these many ones, in talk.'

sentences.t: فَعَلُوا وَقَالُوا أَيُّهَا الْمُخَدَّرَةُ اُرْسُمِي لَنَا بِضَرْبِ رِقَابِهِمْ
sentences.tr: faʿalū wa-qālū: ayyuhā al-mukhaddara, ursumī lanā bi-ḍarbi riqābihim
sentences.l: they did so, and said: 'O secluded lady, decree for us the striking of their necks'
sentences.i: They did so, and said, 'Give the order, my lady — let us strike off their heads.'
sentences.n: The archive prints the masculine vocative أيها before the feminine noun المخدرة, rather than the Classically expected feminine أيتها — another instance, like سبع عبيد earlier in this slice, of this print's loosened gender agreement. مخدّرة is literally a woman kept behind the khidr, the curtained inner chamber of a household — a term for a well-born lady who does not appear before strangers. رسم 'decree' is a bureaucratic verb here, as if she held formal authority over them.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ أَمْهِلُوهُمْ سَاعَةً حَتَّى أَسْأَلَهُمْ عَنْ حَالِهِمْ قَبْلَ ضَرْبِ رِقَابِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat: amhilūhum sāʿatan ḥattā asʾalahum ʿan ḥālihim qabla ḍarbi riqābihim
sentences.l: and she said: 'give them respite an hour, so that I may ask them about their condition before the striking of their necks'
sentences.i: But she said, 'Give them a moment's grace, until I question them about themselves, before their necks are struck.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ يَا سِتْرَ اللَّٰهِ يَا سِتِّي لَا تَقْتُلِينِي بِذَنْبِ غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammāl: yā sitra Allāhi, yā sittī, lā taqtulīnī bi-dhanbi ghayrī
sentences.l: and the porter said: 'O covering of God, O my lady, do not kill me for the sin of another'
sentences.i: The porter said, 'God protect us — my lady, do not kill me for someone else's fault.'
sentences.n: يا ستر الله is a stock cry of alarm ('God shelter us!'), not a literal address. ستّي is the colloquial contraction of سيدتي, 'my lady.'

sentences.t: وَالْجَمِيعُ أَخْطَأُوا وَدَخَلُوا فِي الذَّنْبِ إِلَّا أَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-al-jamīʿu akhṭaʾū wa-dakhalū fī al-dhanbi illā anā
sentences.l: and everyone erred and entered into the fault, except I
sentences.i: Every one of them did wrong and shares the blame — except me.

sentences.t: وَاللَّٰهِ لَقَدْ كَانَتْ لَيْلَتُنَا طَيِّبَةً لَوْ سَلِمْنَا مِنْ هَٰؤُلَاءِ الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ لَوْ دَخَلُوا مَدِينَةً عَامِرَةً أَخْرَبُوهَا
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi laqad kānat laylatunā ṭayyibatan law salimnā min hāʾulāʾi al-qalandariyyati alladhīna law dakhalū madīnatan ʿāmiratan akhrabūhā
sentences.l: by God, our night would have been good, had we been safe from these qalandars, who — if they entered a thriving city — would ruin it
sentences.i: By God, this would have been a fine night, if only we had been spared these qalandars — men who would wreck a flourishing city if they so much as walked into one.
sentences.n: قرندلية, 'qalandars,' are wandering mendicant dervishes; the word is a Persian loan, not a Classical Arabic root.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma yaqūlu shiʿr
sentences.l: then he speaks verse:
sentences.i: Then he recited these lines:
sentences.n: The narrator shifts to the vivid present tense (yaqūlu, 'he says') to introduce the recitation, a common device before verse.

sentences.t:
مَا اَحْسَنَ الْعَفْوَ مِنَ الْقَادِرِ * لَا سِيَّمَا مِنْ غَيْرِ ذِي نَاصِرِ
بِحُرْمَةِ الْوُدِّ الَّذِي بَيْنَنَا * لَا تُفْسِدِ الْاَوَّلَ بِالْاٰخِرِ
sentences.tr:
mā aḥsana al-ʿafwa min al-qādiri * lā siyyamā min ghayri dhī nāṣiri
bi-ḥurmati al-wuddi alladhī baynanā * lā tufsidi al-awwala bi-al-ākhiri
sentences.l:
How fine is pardon from the capable one * especially from one who has no helper.
By the sanctity of the love between us * do not spoil the first with the last.
sentences.i: How fine a thing is mercy from the strong — above all from one who has no protector! By the bond of affection between us, do not let what comes after ruin what has gone before.
sentences.n: لا سيّما ('especially, all the more so') is a fixed idiom. This verse's own vowel points are the archive's own and are kept exactly as printed, letter for letter.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ الْحَمَّالُ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ ضَحِكَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha al-ḥammāl min shiʿrihi ḍaḥikat al-ṣabiyya
sentences.l: and when the porter finished his verse, the young woman laughed

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿan al-kalāmi al-mubāḥ
sentences.l: and morning overtook Shahrazad, and she fell silent from the permitted speech
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazad, and she broke off the tale she had leave to tell.
sentences.n: This is the fixed formula that closes each 'night' throughout the work: dawn arrives and Shahrazad stops the story she had license to tell, to resume the next evening.
